title: An ISMS-Oriented Architecture for Intelligent Property Management Based on ISO/IEC 27001:2022
abstract: The digital transformation of property management has led to the increasing integration of information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. To address these issues, this study proposes an Information Security Management System (ISMS)-oriented architecture for intelligent property management based on ISO/IEC 27001:2022. A standard–process–function mapping method is introduced to transform information security requirements into executable business workflows and system functions. The proposed architecture integrates asset and risk management, security control implementation, supplier and outsourcing management, incident response, audit evidence management, and security metrics within a unified framework. Particular attention is given to the integrated governance of IT, OT, and IoT assets and to the traceability of security activities throughout property management processes. A prototype system is further designed to demonstrate the implementation of the proposed architecture, and functional verification is used to examine its feasibility in typical property management scenarios. The proposed approach provides a systematic method for embedding ISMS requirements into intelligent property management systems and offers a practical reference for property enterprises seeking to improve security governance, audit readiness, and continuous improvement capabilities.

title: Methods for Selecting Data Transmission Network Protocols in Energy Systems
venue: Security of Infocommunication Systems and Internet of Things
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study aimed at enhancing data transmission stability and efficiency in modern energy systems, specifically Smart Grids. The research addresses the critical challenge of optimizing communication protocols within the context of evolving infrastructure and the increasing integration of Distributed Energy Resources. The primary focus of this work is the development of an intelligent communication control system featuring a decision-making mechanism that, based on the analysis of a set of input parameters including network latency, packet loss, and throughput, determines the feasibility of switching between data transmission protocols such as MQTT, CoAP, and HTTPS in real-time. The study employs an ensemble of machine learning classifiers to analyze real-time network telemetry to develop a mechanism for adaptive protocol switching. The proposed methodology integrates the analysis of network traffic dynamics with real-time performance metrics to facilitate dynamic protocol selection. An approach is proposed wherein an ensemble of machine learning models processes a vector of input metrics and classifies the current network state, initiating a protocol switch only when critical threshold values are reached. Experimental validation demonstrates that the adaptive protocol switching system provides improved network traffic scheduling efficiency compared to static implementations. The results indicate significant potential for reducing communication overhead while maintaining high standards of reliability and security in energy system operations. Specifically, the approach prevents data transmission over degraded channels by automatically switching to lightweight protocols like CoAP when connection parameters deteriorate, thereby ensuring compliance with timing requirements. The developed methodology establishes a foundation for the implementation of intelligent communication systems in Smart Grids, contributing to enhanced energy efficiency and grid stability. The findings hold practical value for energy utilities seeking to modernize their infrastructure and optimize data transmission within increasingly complex energy networks.

title: A Multi-Stage Framework for Intrusion Detection and Attack-Path Reconstruction in Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) Networks
abstract: Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) underpins bidirectional communication in smart grids, a foundational layer of smart city energy systems, facilitating the flow of data, real-time monitoring, and demand-responsive control. But its connectivity exposes smart meters to data tampering, denial-of-service attack, and false-data-injection attacks. Most intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for AMI only report that an intrusion has occurred but cannot reconstruct how it propagated or where it originated, leaving the operators without the forensic evidence to perform containment. This paper proposes a multi-stage approach coupling detection with forensic analysis. A recurrent neural network (RNN) extracts temporal features, a support vector classifier (SVC) performs binary classification, and ant colony optimization (ACO) serves two purposes: feature selection before classification and a backward path reconstruction after an intrusion is confirmed. The proposed framework is evaluated on a simulated AMI network with forensic ground truth and further validated on the public UNSW-NB15 benchmark. The detection accuracy exceeds 96%, while ACO reduces the feature set from 40 to 14. A McNemar’s test (p=0.265) indicates that this feature reduction does not significantly alter the per-sample error pattern. With the use of the improved tracer, the Path Overlap Score increases from 0.29 to 0.40, while the False-Positive Path Rate decreases from 0.39 to 0.19, relative to the centroid baseline tracer used for forensic tracking. This improvement in the Path Overlap Score is statistically significant (p=4.39×10−8). However, the Source Localization Rate remains relatively low (9%–11%) for both methods, owing to the intrinsic difficulty of identifying the true source meter from incomplete alert data. Therefore, the proposed framework not only reliably detects intrusions but also significantly outperforms the baseline tracer in path overlap and false-positive rate, although precise source localization remains an open challenge.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Incentive‐Based Demand Response in Energy Markets: Techniques, Challenges, Emerging Trends, and Future Research Directions
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a comprehensive and systematic review of the Incentive‐Based Demand Response (IBDR) program, highlighting its development, design, and implementation in modern Renewable Energy (RE)‐based hierarchical Energy Markets (EMs). The study categorizes the existing body of research into four key domains: EM modeling, optimization techniques, Social Welfare (SW), and uncertainty management, and provides an in‐depth examination of recent advancements and limitations of IBDR programs. Multiple incentive mechanisms are critically examined, which include game‐theoretic frameworks, dynamic incentive schemes, optimization‐based scheduling, and coupon‐driven participation models. The review highlights their comparative effectiveness in reducing load, lowering operational costs, enhancing market efficiency, and stabilizing grid operations under varying demand and RE. The work reviewed recent literature and identified persistent challenges in consumer privacy, scalability, interoperability, and regulatory heterogeneity that continue to obstruct the large‐scale deployment of IBDR programs. By systematically linking IBDR strategies to wind power uncertainty and SW optimization, the review establishes a unified analytical framework largely absent from the existing literature. The future research roadmap highlights emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI) for predictive optimization, blockchain for transparent and secure transactions, and multi‐energy system integration for coordinated Ancillary Services (AS). The study found that IBDR, along with wind uncertainty approaches, is an important program for developing sustainable, resilient, and socially optimized energy systems that align technical innovation with environmental and economic objectives.

title: Engineering Analysis of Half-Hourly Hydropower Plant Records: Operating-Regime Reconstruction, Energy Estimation, and State-Aware Data-Quality Assessment
abstract: Half-hourly hydropower plant records support the engineering analysis of operating states, energy, and measurement consistency; however, legacy spreadsheet structures complicate their integration within a traceable workflow. We analyzed authorized records from an anonymized plant using source-preserving data processing. The workbook comprised 31 sheets and included 1519 rows. Of these, 1488 complete intervals constituted the analytical dataset, with no imputation applied. A common unit-state model was used to reconstruct the operating regimes, allocate the interval energy, and condition the data quality diagnostics. The estimated monthly energy was 3689.75 MWh (119.02 MWh/day). The both-online configuration represented 291.0 allocated hours and accounted for 54.04% of the estimated energy; single-unit configurations represented 435.5 allocated hours; and the both-offline configuration represented 17.5 allocated hours. Daily energy was strongly associated with the mean turbine flow (Pearson’s r = 0.967; Spearman’s rho = 0.950; n = 31). Unit power-factor formula errors coincided with inactive unit states, all 35 negative line-power records occurred while both units were offline, and one interval had a 0.584 MW aggregation discrepancy. By using the reconstructed unit state as a shared analytical layer, the framework links energy allocation and measurement diagnostics while preserving record-level provenance. title: Federated Edge Learning for Privacy-Preserving Energy Monitoring and Control in Electric Vehicle Networks
venue: International Conference on Computing, Intelligence, and Application (CIACON)
abstract: Electric Vehicle (EV) charging networks generate session logs and control traces. Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) supports monitoring and scheduling at the edge. Raw multisite pooling can expose user routines. Station heterogeneity also makes a single centralized model unreliable for local control. Conventional approaches either train centrally or use fixed rulebased schedulers. Central training requires uploads, while rules adapt poorly to changing demand. Federated Learning (FL) enables cross-station training without moving raw data. Each client uses a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) plus Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) model, aggregated with Federated Averaging (FedAvg). Differential Privacy (DP) is optionally applied to client updates to bound disclosure risk. This design targets monitoring and control in distributed charging infrastructure. Experiments use Adaptive Charging Network Data (ACN-Data) from Caltech and Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The benchmark includes more than 30,000 sessions with 4-second sampling of pilotSignal and chargingCurrent. For delivered-energy prediction, localonly learning attains Mean Absolute Error (MAE) 2.41 kWh. Personalized FedAvg reduces MAE to 1.58 kWh and achieves $\mathbf{1 7. 4} \boldsymbol{\%}$ peak reduction with $\mathbf{6. 4} \mathbf{~ m i n}$ delay. The framework suits workplace and fleet charging where coordination is needed under data restrictions. Tighter DP budgets reduce utility, so privacy parameters must be chosen per deployment.

title: A Computer Vision techniques and Transformer-Based Framework for Short-Term Energy Consumption Forecasting in Smart Grids
abstract: Accurate short-term energy consumption forecasting is critical for the efficient operation of smart grids to balance the loads in advance, implement demand response on the consumer side, and reduce distribution costs. However, most of the existing deep learning methods, including LSTMs and CNN-based models, are unable to capture both long-range temporal patterns and the fine-grained local patterns within high-resolution smart meter data simultaneously. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical transformer-based framework called EF-Transformer for short-term energy forecasting, which consists of a multi-scale patch embedding module, a dual-branch temporal attention encoder, and an adaptive decomposition gate that decomposes and handles non-stationary trend and seasonal components. We evaluate the proposed model on three publicly available benchmark datasets, including the UCI Individual Household Electric Power Consumption dataset, the Electricity Load Diagrams 2011-2014 dataset, and the Smart Meter Energy Consumption dataset, and on the UCI household dataset, EF-Transformer achieves the best MAE of 0.091 kWh, RMSE of 0.134 kWh, and MAPE of 2.87% among the state-of-the-art models, including LSTM, Auto former, Informer, and Patch-TST. We conduct ablation experiments to demonstrate that all the components of the architecture contribute to the state-of-the-art performance, and overall, EF-Transformer provides a scalable and interpretable solution for smart grid operators who require accurate short-term consumption forecasts at both household and grid levels.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Service-Enriched EV and Building Flexibility Contracts in Distribution Feeders
abstract: Electric-vehicle (EV) charging and flexible building loads can increase or relieve distribution-level loading and voltage stress, depending on timing, placement, and flexibility. This paper empirically evaluates a shared service-enriched flexibility-contract representation for coordinating EV departure-energy service and building comfort service. Individual EV and building records encode service limits, deadlines or comfort bounds, and feeder locations. The evaluation compares uncontrolled, service-constrained, feeder-aware, and heuristic uncertainty-aware control, with inputs from empirical residuals or split-conformal scalar service-score quantiles. In the simplified study, 256 scenarios under four modes produce 1024 evaluations. Realized nominal EV energy shortfall and building comfort violations are zero in the tested scenarios, while a separate earlier-departure stress audit shows heuristic uncertainty-aware tightening reducing EV stress-risk cases from 106 to 64. Open Distribution System Simulator (OpenDSS) audits on IEEE 123 and IEEE 34 each include 2048 scenarios and 8192 evaluations; stress-risk cases fall from 1005 to 536, with mean peak tradeoffs of 17.66 kW and 18.26 kW. A reduced-information experiment compares raw-state, individual-contract, and noisy/coarsened information-view proxies for exposure and payload rather than formal privacy. The results provide bounded empirical evidence that service-enriched EV/building contracts can expose service-grid and information-view tradeoffs in the tested simplified and OpenDSS feeder studies and audits.

title: Distributed electricity–carbon co-optimization of hydrogen energy storage microgrids with dynamic laplace perturbation and model predictive control
abstract: Hydrogen energy storage microgrids can improve renewable-energy accommodation and cross-energy flexibility, while repeated boundary-variable exchange in distributed scheduling may expose private operating information. This paper develops a privacy-aware electricity-carbon co-optimization framework that integrates day-ahead distributed clearing with intra-day model predictive control (MPC). The day-ahead model coordinates electricity, heat, hydrogen conversion, battery storage, and thermal storage while accounting for direct gas-boiler emissions and indirect emissions associated with imported electricity. A dynamically decaying Laplace mechanism is incorporated into the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and privacy performance is evaluated through finite-transcript privacy-budget accounting and reconstruction-based leakage analysis. Compared with fixed Laplace noise, the dynamic mechanism exhibits a higher baseline mean leakage-risk score (0.67 versus 0.58), but reduces the centralized cost gap from 2.85% to 0.94% and the number of iterations from 50 to 38. Matched-condition tests further show lower cost gaps at equal leakage risk and lower leakage risk at equal cost gap. An inverse-variance reconstruction attack reveals increased information exposure during later iterations. Meanwhile, the intra-day MPC maintains feasible multi-energy operation under the tested forecast errors. The base-case operational emissions are 2.09 t CO2, and the carbon-parameter sensitivity analysis shows a smooth variation in cleared cost. The results demonstrate the coordinated economic, privacy, and convergence characteristics of the proposed scheduling framework.

title: AAIGF-E: An AI and Agentic Intelligence Governance Framework for Electric-Sector Smart-City Infrastructure
abstract: AI is being deployed in smart-grid and smart-city energy infrastructure faster than governance frameworks can validate it. Existing instruments—NERC CIP, NIST AI RMF 1.0, and ISA/IEC 62443—address cybersecurity compliance and AI trustworthiness principles but do not provide operational control architecture for AI systems influencing grid stability, distributed energy resource (DER) dispatch, or real-time reliability decisions. Compliance with these instruments is not equivalent to operational assurance: their requirements do not by themselves establish validated input integrity controls, adversarial robustness testing, or bounded autonomy architecture for every AI-enabled operational use case. This paper presents the AI and Agentic Intelligence Governance Framework, Electric Sector (AAIGF-E): 111 controls across seven lifecycle phases (Govern, Design, Implement, Assure, Monitor, Respond, Recover), mapped to existing electric-sector compliance obligations. A defining structural feature of AAIGF-E is its dual-narrative control architecture, in which each control carries both an AI governance rationale and a parallel electric-sector operational translation, enabling the framework to serve AI governance stakeholders and operational technology (OT) engineering teams within the same control set without requiring cross-discipline translation. Scenario-driven validation tests the framework against three operationally relevant failure modes: adversarial manipulation of DER dispatch AI, unauthorized autonomous action execution by an agentic AI system in an OT environment, and silent model drift in grid stability forecasting. Validation confirms structural coverage across prevention, detection, and response phases and identifies residual implementation and assurance gaps while identifying a residual prompt-injection pathway in which technically valid operational content may manipulate agent task scope or apparent authority before downstream actuation controls activate. The 111-control register is further characterized through quantitative analysis of standards coverage, lifecycle and governance-domain distribution, cross-framework convergence, and sector-specific translation. A separate independent coding reproducibility check samples 35 controls across five reference frameworks, producing 175 binary mapping decisions; 155 decisions agree with the internal coding key (88.6% raw agreement; Cohen’s κ=0.742). To reduce reliance on author-led validation, a representative operational scenario is also evaluated by independent AI governance, cybersecurity, and ICS/OT experts who derive their judgments before reviewing the AAIGF-E reference assessment. Their domain selections and governance recommendations show strong overall convergence with the framework assessment. AAIGF-E is designed for electric utilities and smart-city operators within North American regulatory frameworks who need governance architecture that connects AI lifecycle risk management to existing compliance cycles rather than replacing them.

title: Bit-Rate Allocation for Quantized Kalman Filtering via Rate-Distortion Theory
abstract: The performance of Kalman filters in networked sensing systems is often limited by communication bandwidth, making quantization unavoidable. This paper studies a centralized quantized Kalman filtering framework in which a local central processor communicates state information to a remote central processor through a bandwidth-constrained channel. Motivated by sensing architectures with high-accuracy meters and local processing capabilities, the measurements are modeled as direct quantized versions of the system states. Under this setting, the proposed framework allocates a fixed communication budget among correlated state variables using the Gaussian rate–distortion function for independent sources. State correlations are exploited through a basis determined by the system dynamics and innovation covariance, enabling an analytically tractable reverse-water-filling allocation while maintaining a low-complexity scalar-quantization architecture. A steady-state analysis identifies the appropriate operating basis for four classes of dynamical systems and yields a practical covariance-aware allocation procedure. Since the allocation relies on moment-matched Gaussian approximations of the posterior and predicted prior distributions, their accuracy is assessed through Kullback-Leibler divergence analysis. Simulations show close agreement between theory and practical scalar quantization, and comparisons against uniform and random baselines demonstrate substantial distortion reductions, with improvements above 95% in the reported ill-conditioned systems. The results show that covariance-aware communication-budget allocation can significantly improve estimation performance with low implementation complexity.

title: A Holistic Comparative Study of AI Models for Reliable Household Energy Consumption Forecasting
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into various critical areas of our daily life like autonomous vehicles, energy, healthcare, defense, manufacturing, and finance to improve efficiency and automation. Thus, it is paramount to model and evaluate the reliability of AI methods, ensuring that AI systems in those critical applications are safe, accountable and capable of functioning efficiently as expected. This article puts forward a straightforward, comprehensive reliability index that integrates seven performance metrics spanning accuracy, efficiency, and robustness to evaluate and compare the performance of AI methods. The sequential least squares programming algorithm is employed to optimize the weights of different metrics under application-specific constraints, facilitating fair comparisons across applications with different operational requirements. Based on the proposed index with the optimized weights, a set of 35 AI methods are studied and compared, including cutting-edge time series forecasting methods (e.g., random forest, long short-term memory (LSTM), TimeMixer), and hybrid methods (e.g., convolutional neural network-LSTM, empirical wavelet transform-LSTM, empirical mode decomposition-LSTM, variational mode decomposition-LSTM, stationary wavelet transform-LSTM, and singular spectrum analysis-LSTM). Empirical studies of those AI methods using the U.K.-DALE household datasets are conducted, revealing that the stationary wavelet transform-LSTM is a top-performing model with strong generalizability and stability for example applications in short-term household energy consumption forecasting. The proposed index serves as a valuable tool for selecting reliable AI models to be deployed in critical applications.

title: A Mixture of Experts Method with Coordinated Imputation for Multi-Residential Load Forecasting under Missing Data
venue: IEEE Power Engineering Society General Meeting
abstract: Residential smart-meter data are often incomplete, and training a dedicated forecasting model for each residence is impractical. In this context, this paper proposes a mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework for residential load forecasting under missing data and large user populations. The proposed MoE comprises multiple imputation–forecasting coordinated experts and a gating neural network. For any load series with missing data, the series is fed in parallel to all experts and the gating network, which assigns routing weights based on electricity consumption patterns rather than residence IDs, thereby enabling pattern-level knowledge sharing across users. Each imputation-forecasting coordinate expert consists of a bidirectional recurrent imputation for time series model (BRITS)-based imputer and a long short-term memory neural network (LSTM)-based forecaster, which is optimized through a coordinated experts’ loss function considering both interpolation accuracy and the impact of imputation. The forecasting results of each expert will be weighed according to the weight of gating NN and then aggregated to output. The simulation results in a public residential load dataset verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Electricity demand anomaly detection and forecasting: a hybrid framework for improved grid management
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a robust and interpretable forecasting framework for short-term electricity demand that supports sustainable energy demand management, particularly under conditions of demand volatility and unexpected events. Design/methodology/approach This study proposes a hybrid Prophet-XGBoost forecasting framework that combines a decomposable time-series model with machine learning–based residual learning. The model was validated using 425 days of operational data from the Taiwan Power Company, utilizing a 30-day out-of-sample test set to simulate real-world forecasting. Findings The hybrid model consistently improves upon the standalone Prophet baseline and remains highly competitive with standalone XGBoost. Anomaly detection identifies demand irregularities linked to exogenous shocks, such as national holidays, improving robustness and interpretability. Practical implications The framework offers energy utilities and system operators a practical decision-support tool for improving short-term load forecasting, anticipating demand shocks, and strengthening grid reliability. Originality/value This study contributes a decision-oriented hybrid forecasting framework that combines statistical interpretability with machine learning accuracy and explicit anomaly detection for energy sector management.

title: Data-driven Control of Distributed Energy Resources in Virtual Power Plants Under Uncertainty
venue: IEEE Power Engineering Society General Meeting
abstract: This study presents a data-driven control methodology for managing distributed energy resources (DERs)—specifically battery energy storage systems (BESS) and photovoltaic (PV) units—to improve the operational performance and reliability of virtual power plants (VPPs). Instead of relying on an explicit mathematical model, the proposed controller utilizes historical input–output measurements to coordinate the actions of BESS, PV units, and electric vehicles (EVs) under uncertain and variable operating conditions. To handle uncertainty and operational constraints, a predictive optimization layer is incorporated, enabling the controller to adjust in real time to fluctuations in grid conditions. By using actual household demand, PV generation, and EV charging data, the approach accurately reflects system behavior without the need for detailed parameter estimation or model identification. Extensive simulations on a European low-voltage distribution test feeder demonstrate that the controller can efficiently schedule PV and BESS resources while achieving substantial improvements in voltage regulation. The results verify the method’s robustness, scalability, and suitability for practical real-time deployment in modern distribution networks with high renewable and EV integration.

title: The techno-regulatory trilemma: A global taxonomy of electricity tariff transitions
abstract: As the global power sector transitions toward a decentralized and decarbonized Era 4.0, legacy electricity pricing mechanisms increasingly fail to align with shifting marginal system costs. This paper challenges the universal advocacy for real-time pricing (RTP) by proposing the Techno-Regulatory Trilemma, a novel framework that models tariff design as a dynamic equilibrium between infrastructural maturity, generation profiles, and socio-economic objectives. By establishing a comprehensive taxonomy of six fundamental archetypes across four evolutionary eras, we provide a global roadmap for tariff migration supported by a continental-scale empirical analysis of over 200 global jurisdictions. Our findings elucidate the green zone and red zone dynamics, revealing that 54.7% of the analyzed jurisdictions currently remain tethered to constrained static regimes. We argue that the retention of static mechanisms in resource-constrained environments is not a failure of innovation but a rational optimization to ensure revenue adequacy. The core contribution of this research is the formulation of the strategic equilibrium, offering a definitive diagnostic tool for policymakers to navigate complex regulatory landscapes. Ultimately, this framework ensures that future electricity markets remain resilient, economically viable, and socially equitable, providing a foundational guide for utility regulation in the decentralized age.

title: VERS UNE SECURITE LEGERE ET EVOLUTIVE DES INFRASTRUCTURES DE COMPTAGE AVANCE : UNE ARCHITECTURE FONDEE SUR LA CRYPTOGRAPHIE A COURBES ELLIPTIQUES
abstract: Securing advanced metering infrastructures (AMI) requires mutual authentication, confidentiality, fine-grained revocation, and low overhead on constrained devices. Because combining asymmetric cryptography for trust establishment with symmetric cryptography for recurring traffic is already a standard design principle, this study focuses on a more specific contribution: the specification and evaluation of a complete AMI protocol based on P-256/ECDSA/ECDH, HKDF-SHA-256, and AES-GCM, with transcript binding, nonces, an anti-replay counter, key confirmation, renewal, revocation, reconnection, and firmware verification. The evaluation combines security-equivalent parameter comparison, reproducible software micro-benchmarks, and a massive-reconnection load simulation. At roughly 128 bits of classical security, a compressed P-256 public key reduces raw size by 91.4% relative to RSA-3072, while an ECDSA signature reduces it by 83.3%. On the reference platform, ECDSA signing averaged 0.024 ms versus 0.813 ms for RSA-PSS-3072, and the HES-side ECC handshake core reached about 5.2 × 10^3 authentications/s per worker. However, a burst of 10^6 reconnections within 10 s saturates five workers, producing a P95 latency of about 27 s. ECC therefore improves compactness, but scalability also depends on server provisioning and burst control; a hybrid, crypto-agile architecture remains necessary.

title: International Comparison of Smart Meter Solutions and Functionalities in Europe
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of smart meter (SM) solutions and functionalities across Europe, with a particular focus on Germany and Spain. Smart meters (SMs) serve as the technological backbone, enabling granular consumption insights, automated data exchange, demand response participation, integration of distributed energy resources, and system-wide optimization. Despite harmonized EU-level provisions such as Directive (EU) 2019/944 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1162, national implementations within the EU remain fragmented, resulting in limited interoperability and high integration costs. Through detailed mapping of EU legislation and in-depth country profiling, the study evaluates national SM infrastructures with a particular focus on governance structures, technical architectures, and data access principles. Germany serves as an example of a highly complex, secure gateway-based architecture with advanced flexibility features, but faces challenges in market adoption and scalability. Spain showcases a rapid, DSO-centric rollout with high penetration rates but limited consumer empowerment and interface standardization. The analysis identifies key barriers to harmonization, including divergent market roles, data availability, and security models, which impede the scalability of smart energy services. The paper concludes that a unified regulatory and technical approach, standardizing roles, data formats, interfaces, and certification, is essential for achieving interoperability, scalability, and the full benefits of smart metering across Europe.

title: Trust-Aware Federated Deep Learning for Network Anomaly Detection Under Non-IID Data
abstract: Distributed network systems produce complex traffic flows that are hard to analyze with a centralized architecture of Intrusion Detection Systems. Traffic distributions are different between participating edge nodes, and it can involve sharing sensitive traffic information and require more communication. A trust-aware federated anomaly detection framework based on a Hybrid Long Short-Term Memory Autoencoder is proposed to detect anomalies in networks with non-independent and identically distributed data. To avoid divergence from local data, FedProx is integrated with the client-side optimization, and to avoid the impact of low-confidence model updates, trust-aware aggregation is employed. The experimental study is based on the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 intrusion dataset where the clients are unequally partitioned, and the performance of convergence, communication cost, non-IID performance, energy consumption, and detection metrics are evaluated. Better detection performance is noted using the proposed system than the baseline models.

title: Optimizing energy storage in microgrids under uncertainty: Balancing reliability, cost, and battery wear
abstract: Smart microgrids integrating renewable energy sources are important to sustainable energy development, but their stable and economic operation is challenged by the uncertainty and intermittency of renewable generation. This paper formulates a chance-constrained stochastic energy-management model that explicitly accounts for correlated renewable uncertainties. The model minimizes total operational cost, including grid-energy purchases and battery degradation, while ensuring high-probability satisfaction of power-balance and system constraints. A partial sample average approximation framework is developed to reduce computational complexity relative to conventional sample average approximation by avoiding excessive scenario-dependent binary variables. Numerical simulations on a modified IEEE 9-bus microgrid show that, for the same 1000-scenario case, the proposed method reduces solution time from 300 s to 45 s, corresponding to an approximately 85% reduction. Its operating cost remains within 1.5% of that obtained from a much larger 10,000-scenario sample average approximation used only as a near-exact reference solution. Battery participation further reduces operating cost by up to 15%, decreases equipment switching, and improves voltage profiles by 5%–10%. These results demonstrate an efficient approach for storage-aware microgrid scheduling under correlated renewable uncertainty, while validation on larger network topologies and longer planning horizons remains an important direction for future work.

title: Development of an Automated IoT-based System for Monitoring and Control of Electrical Energy Consumption
abstract: The article addresses the problem of monitoring and control of electrical energy consumption using Internet of Things technologies. A conceptual architecture of an automated system integrating electrical parameter measurement devices, microcontroller-based control, wireless communication technologies, cloud services, and remote load management mechanisms is proposed. Existing energy monitoring solutions are analyzed, and their major limitations related to insufficient integration of automatic control functions, high deployment costs, and dependence on proprietary platforms are identified. The general system architecture and automation structure are developed based on a closed-loop control system with negative feedback. The residential electrical network is considered as the controlled object, while active power consumption is selected as the controlled variable. A measurement subsystem based on the HLW8032 energy metering integrated circuit is proposed for real-time acquisition of voltage, current, power, and energy consumption parameters. Algorithms for data acquisition, transmission, processing, and automated load disconnection under overload conditions are developed. The proposed approach can be applied to the development of intelligent energy management systems for residential and small-scale commercial applications. Experimental validation and performance evaluation of the developed system are considered as subjects of future research.

title: Motivations and Challenges in Deploying Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) within Smart Grids
venue: The University of Ha’il Journal of Science (UOHJS)
abstract: Climate change mitigation strategies require the wider adoption of renewable energy sources for electricity generation and mobility. The intermittency of renewable generation cannot be handled by conventional grids, leading to power quality issues. A flexible energy management system is therefore required to support the increasing incorporation of renewables in the system. Smart grids can enable the adoption of renewables by facilitating the management of electricity through automated control and continuous monitoring. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) in smart grids can charge during times of low demand when energy is generated in excess, and discharge during times of high demand providing key services such as frequency regulation, peak shaving, renewable firming, and emergency grid support. Hence, BESS is an integral part of smart grids. The study analyses the role of BESS in empowering smart grids and the motivations and barriers to the adoption of BESS. Case studies of BESS-integrated smart grids are also analysed to understand the motivations and barriers.

title: Digitalising Energy: Navigating the Protection of Consumer Rights and Privacy in Malaysia
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: The digitalisation of the energy sector, driven by technologies such as smart infrastructure, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and AI-powered energy management systems, has transformed the way consumers interact with energy services. While these technologies offer greater efficiency and convenience, they also raise important legal concerns regarding consumer data privacy, transparency, informed consent, and data security. This article examines the legal implications of digital energy technologies, with particular attention to how energy providers collect, process, and use consumer data and the risks associated with data security breaches. Using doctrinal and comparative legal methods, the article analyses Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (PDPA), including the reforms introduced by the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024, against the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The analysis assesses whether Malaysia’s post-amendment framework adequately protects consumers against the privacy risks associated with increasingly data-driven energy services. Although the recent amendments have strengthened Malaysia’s data protection framework, several regulatory concerns remain, particularly in relation to transparency, consumer control over personal data, and the governance of emerging digital technologies. The article concludes that further sector-specific safeguards and effective enforcement mechanisms are necessary to strengthen consumer autonomy, privacy, and data security in Malaysia’s digital energy sector.

title: Design and Implementation of a Novel Laboratory Stand for Teaching IoT
venue: European Journal of Applied Science Engineering and Technology
abstract: This work prioritizes the implementation of laboratory experiments using real-world experimental components. A new laboratory stand concept is proposed for hands-on learning of IoT technologies, and the functionality of an IoT stand based on real-world components is discussed. The proposed approach combines laboratory-based learning with the use of real-world components, enabling students to progress from studying individual IoT components to designing and implementing complete IoT systems. The laboratory stand is designed as a modular platform that supports different sensors and actuators and enables students to perform experiments focused on system architecture, data collection, monitoring, and control. The proposed platform is based on a Raspberry Pi 5 server, Zigbee communication, a Wi-Fi network, and software tools including Home Assistant, Zigbee2MQTT, and Grafana. The stand allows students to independently configure sensors and actuators, design the architecture of an IoT system, and conduct experiments using real-world devices. Several educational courses were developed using the proposed laboratory stand, and the results of student surveys indicate positive perceptions regarding the development of independent learning and problem-solving skills, as well as the ability to apply theoretical knowledge in practice. The study demonstrates the high functional capabilities of the real-world IoT stand and its strong potential for practical applications. The proposed solution can support not only individual laboratory experiments but also the implementation of complete technological processes with comprehensive parameter monitoring and control. Furthermore, the integration of multiple laboratory stands can extend the platform to support advanced educational and research activities.

title: Topology-aware Orchestration of Distributed Energy Resources in Blockchain-enabled Virtual Power Plants
venue: International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
abstract: Most Virtual Power Plant (VPP) coordination approaches rely on centralized architectures that assume complete energy system visibility and trusted coordination entities, while neglecting the topology and local grid constraints introduced by high penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs). This paper presents a decentralized VPP orchestration framework that relies on a hierarchical structure to align energy resource aggregation and dispatch, with the grid structure to enable topology-aware coordination. The framework offers an orchestration service based on a tailored genetic optimization algorithm with a multi-objective fitness function addressing energy amount, cost, and topology. DERs are coordinated through a market mechanism in which procurement bids and orders initiate VPPs and offers are aggregated into a tree rooted at the Point of Common Coupling. A blockchain-based coordination layer with smart contracts allows for trustful DERs registration, monitoring, settlement and payment. The orchestration service has insights into grid topology and real-time monitored data and uses a grid topology-aware optimization algorithm to generate the VPP configuration that is enforced through blockchain smart contracts. Evaluation using DERs from a benchmark distribution network demonstrates that the proposed approach can effectively construct VPPs while satisfying multi-criteria objectives, taking advantage of blockchain smart contracts that ensure secure and transparent settlement and verification.

title: CA-AFiD: A Context-Aware Adaptive Federated Intrusion Diagnosis for Heterogeneous IoT–Fog–Cloud Environments
abstract: The increasing heterogeneity of Internet of Things (IoT) environments makes intrusion diagnosis challenging because device behaviours, traffic patterns, and attack distributions can vary across deployment conditions, while data-locality requirements limit centralized access to network data. This study proposes CA-AFiD (Context-Aware Adaptive Federated Intrusion Diagnosis), a framework designed to support adaptive and interpretable intrusion diagnosis across IoT–Fog–Cloud environments. CA-AFiD combines behaviour-aware representation learning using Transformer, BiLSTM, and attention mechanisms with a context-aware adaptive ensemble that adjusts learner contributions according to behavioural complexity, attack density, and device context. Federated learning is used to coordinate model updates across distributed Fog nodes without sharing raw traffic data, while attention-based interpretation, SHAP feature attribution, and ATT&CK-oriented contextualization provide explanatory information for diagnostic decisions. The framework was evaluated on the CIC-IoT-DIAD 2024 dataset across device-aware learning, imbalanced attack diagnosis, temporal sensitivity, federated learning, explainability, and operational-efficiency scenarios. Under the controlled homogeneous evaluation, the complete CA-AFiD framework achieved a 99.22% F1-score, while the heterogeneous evaluation achieved an overall 99.03% F1-score across the evaluated attack categories. Across the four evaluated minority attack categories, the average F1-score was 98.79%. Under federated learning, the global model achieved an average device-identification accuracy of 98.90% and an average anomaly-diagnosis F1-score of 98.90% across the participating Fog nodes, while ATT&CK mapping achieved 88–98% coverage. These results demonstrate the potential of CA-AFiD to provide adaptive, data-local, and interpretable intrusion diagnosis for heterogeneous IoT–Fog–Cloud environments.

title: Grid-Scale Energy Storage Deployment and Operational Challenges in the Saudi Electric Power System: A Review
abstract: Saudi Arabia is expanding renewable energy and grid-scale storage as part of the modernization of its power sector. Solar and wind power can reduce dependence on fossil fuel generation, but their variable output adds operational challenges related to ramping, reserve planning, voltage and frequency control, renewable curtailment, and peak demand management. This paper reviews how energy storage can support renewable energy integration in the Saudi power grid, with attention to reliability, flexibility, storage technologies, smart grid readiness, policy and regulation, techno-economic considerations, and local operating conditions. A structured narrative review was conducted using international peer-reviewed literature together with authoritative Saudi technical, regulatory, policy, and project sources. The review indicates that storage should be evaluated according to the grid service delivered, rather than installed capacity alone. Battery energy storage systems can provide fast grid support services, including frequency response, voltage support, renewable smoothing, reserve support, ramp-rate control, and short-duration energy shifting. Longer-duration options, such as flow batteries, thermal storage, compressed air storage, gravity storage, and hydrogen-linked pathways, may also be useful for bulk shifting and wider balancing needs when technical, economic, and site conditions are suitable. However, storage is not a direct substitute for grid reinforcement, firm generation, demand response, forecasting, or smart grid control. Its value depends on response time, discharge duration, usable energy capacity, converter capability, state-of-charge management, thermal management, degradation, dispatch rules, and cost of service delivery. The review identifies several challenges relevant to Saudi Arabia, including high ambient temperature, dust and soiling, cooling-driven demand, battery degradation, storage sizing and siting, forecasting accuracy, market rules, cybersecurity, and performance verification. Future research should give greater attention to hot-climate battery performance, renewable and load forecasting, optimal siting, storage service valuation, forecasting-linked dispatch, hybrid storage options, and coordination between storage systems and smart grid infrastructure.

title: An Improved Informer-Based Load Forecasting Method Incorporating Electricity Consumption Profiling
abstract: Accurate demand-side load forecasting is essential for reliable power system operation, energy management, and demand-side decision-making. However, heterogeneous electricity-use behavior among residential users and multiscale temporal variations remain major challenges for conventional forecasting models. To address these issues, this study develops an electricity-use-aware load forecasting method that integrates user behavior profiling with an improved Informer model. First, symbolic aggregate approximation (SAX) and hierarchical clustering are employed to extract representative load patterns from residential electricity consumption data. LightGBM is then used to identify informative questionnaire attributes associated with different load patterns, and the clustering results and selected user attributes are jointly used to construct multidimensional electricity-use behavior profiles. These profiles provide additional behavioral information for subsequent load forecasting. On this basis, the Informer architecture is improved through three strategies: a temporal convolutional network (TCN)-based embedding for multiscale periodic feature extraction, probabilistic block-sampling attention for local temporal dependency modeling, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP)-based cross-self-attention decoder for nonlinear feature interaction and fusion. Experiments on data from 3207 residential users show that the proposed model achieves an MAE of 0.0237, an RMSE of 0.0258, and an R2 of 0.945. Compared with the original Informer, MAE and RMSE are reduced by 17.4% and 19.8%, respectively, while R2 is increased by 6.65%. The model also outperforms Transformer and LSTM baselines, and the ablation results demonstrate the complementary contributions of the three architectural improvements. These results indicate that combining electricity-use behavior profiling with multiscale temporal modeling can effectively improve residential demand-side load forecasting.

title: TimeGPT vs. LSTM-CNN for Photovoltaic Energy Forecasting
venue: International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
abstract: The large-scale deployment of renewable energy sources at the grid edge has significantly increased the complexity of energy management. In this context, accurate solar energy forecasting is essential, yet challenging due to the intermittent and stochastic nature of photovoltaic generation. Recently, foundation time-series models such as TimeGPT have emerged as a promising alternative paradigm to deep learning approaches. In this paper, we compare the PV energy production forecasting performance of a hybrid deep learning model combining Long Short-Term Memory and Convolutional Neural Network (LSTM-CNN) and TimeGPT. We define an evaluation methodology based on two different input history lengths: a long-term history of one year and a short-term history of one month. For each model, forecasts are generated for three prediction horizons: 24, 72 and 120 hours ahead. This allows for analyzing the models performance under varying temporal contexts, allowing to determine both short and long terms dependencies. Results show that even with extended historical context, TimeGPT performs better in short-term forecasting (24 hours), while LSTM-CNN achieves higher accuracy for medium horizons of (72 / 120 hours) due to explicit sequential modeling.

title: Short-Term Load Forecasting in Smart Distribution Networks: A Systematic Review of Data Analytics, Clustering Techniques, and Forecasting Models
abstract: The operation and management of Smart Distribution Networks (SDNs) heavily relies on the Short-Term Load Forecasting (STLF) function in the context of Demand-Side Management (DSM), Distributed Energy Resource (DER) integration, and grid reliability. With the wide use of smart meters and Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI), it is now possible to obtain high-resolution electricity consumption data, which has opened up new opportunities for data-driven forecasting at the transformer, feeder, substation, and consumer levels. Forecasting in SDNs, however, still faces difficulties because of the variability of the loads, the heterogeneity of the data, the distributed nature of the energy resources, and the stochastic behavior of consumers. This paper provides a systematic literature review of clustering-based and data-driven STLF methodologies for Smart Distribution Systems (SDNs). According to PRISMA guidelines, publications from 2018 to March 2026 were retrieved from Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science and analyzed in terms of clustering techniques, forecasting methods, data sources, and fields of application. The focus is on K-Means, K-Medoids, Hierarchical Clustering, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), and DBSCAN, along with statistical, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Federated Learning (FL), and Edge-computing forecasting frameworks. The review indicates that the clustering-based preprocessing is highly useful in the field of characterizing and forecasting load profiles. In the reviewed studies, DL models, especially LSTM, GRU and CNN models, were repeatedly found to perform better than statistical and ML baseline architectures in their respective experimental scenarios, while FL and edge-computing methods show promise for real-time and privacy-preserving forecasting. Lastly, the review presents existing problems and future research directions on how to create scalable, intelligent, and privacy-preserving forecasting systems in SDNs.

title: Data-Driven Digital Monitoring Framework for Redox Flow Batteries in Cyber-Physical Power Systems
venue: IEEE International Conference on Electronics, Computing and Communication Technologies (CONECCT)
abstract: RFBs are finding increasing applications in gridscale energy storage owing to their scalability, long cycle life, and the decoupling of power and energy. However, for RFB systems to perform reliably under future power grids with cyber-physical infrastructure, continuous monitoring and cyber-physical visibility are unattainable by mere electrochemical modeling. The paper describes a data-driven digital monitoring framework for RFB systems that capitalizes on real-time operational data to facilitate system-level situational awareness. Such a framework integrates physical sensing, data pipeline management, and analytics-driven monitoring in the setting of a cyber-physical system framework. The analytics applies lightweight and interpretable analytics in order to drive the derivation of monitoring variables from the electrical, thermal, state, and auxiliary variables without predictive or control optimization. The framework is validated through multi-month operational data. Such a framework offers a pragmatic approach toward the fully immersive digital monitoring of RFB systems in future cyber-physical power grids.

title: IoT-Enabled Machine Learning-based Fairness-Aware Demand Side Management for Residential Smart Grids
venue: International Conference on Secure Information Systems and Technologies (ICSIST)
abstract: The penetration of smart appliances and electrified residential loads has resulted in the increased peak demand in distribution networks. The traditional Demand Side Management (DSM) techniques are mainly proactive, using threshold based load shedding which disconnects entire load categories resulting in inefficient energy usage and unfair consumer participation. In this paper, we propose an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled machine learning based fairness-aware DSM framework for smart residential communities. The framework integrates Support Vector Regression (SVR)-based peak demand forecasting and granular load selection for proactive peak clipping decision making. A fairness-aware load selection algorithm is proposed to find the minimum number of flexible loads to be curtailed and to ensure the fair participation of residential consumers for demand reduction. Fairness is measured using Jain’s Fairness Index and a fairness accumulator that tracks historic participation. The results obtained using MATLAB/Simulink show that the proposed framework can substantially decrease peak demand and increase fairness as compared to conventional DSM strategies.

title: Green Energy Microgrid Dispatching: A Hybrid Framework of Improved Genetic Algorithm and Reinforcement Learning
venue: Journal of Applied Mathematics and Physics
abstract: High renewable penetration turns microgrid dispatching from an optimization problem into an uncertainty management one. Solar and wind outputs flicker; load demand wavers without rhythm. Both economic efficiency and operational stability come under threat. Conventional methods fall into two camps: model-based approaches, brittle against parameter errors, and search-heavy algorithms, too sluggish for real-time shifts. Neither manages to reconcile global exploration with instantaneous responsiveness—the very balance that dynamic environments demand. To address these issues, this paper proposes a hybrid intelligent optimization framework that integrates an improved genetic algorithm and deep reinforcement learning, aiming to achieve real-time economic dispatching of microgrids with a high proportion of renewable energy. At the algorithmic level, an adaptive hybrid encoding strategy is designed to unify the representation of continuous control variables and discrete equipment states; further, a dynamic mutation mechanism based on deep reinforcement learning is introduced, enabling the algorithm to adjust the mutation probability in real time according to the degree of load disturbance, enhancing the system’s robustness in sudden conditions. At the optimization mechanism level, a DRL-driven fitness evaluation system is constructed: the deep reinforcement learning agent obtains real-time reward signals through interaction with the environment and uses these signals to dynamically modify the fitness function of the genetic algorithm, thereby achieving collaborative optimization of global exploration and local fine search. Simulation results based on the NREL OpenEI Commercial Building and Microgrid Reference Datasets (2018-2022) and the IEEE 33-node system show that, compared with traditional genetic algorithms, Deep Q-Network (DQN), and particle swarm algorithms, the proposed method performs exceptionally well in multiple key indicators: compared to traditional genetic algorithms, the average daily comprehensive operating cost is reduced by 16.3%; compared to particle swarm algorithms, the penetration rate of renewable energy increases by 8.7%; the convergence speed is increased by 20% (based on the genetic algorithm as the benchmark). Moreover, in load disturbance scenarios, the dynamic mutation strategy reduces the cost fluctuation amplitude by 25.0%, demonstrating excellent dynamic adaptability and robustness.

title: A Physics-Inspired Spiking Neural Network for Explainable Decision-Support in Power Grid Operation
venue: International Conference on Data-driven Optimization of Complex Systems (DOCS)
abstract: The rapid integration of renewable energy introduces unprecedented stochasticity to modern power grids, necessitating a paradigm shift from deterministic state prediction to reliable operational risk assessment. In this paper, we propose a novel Neuro-symbolic Closed-loop Learning Framework designed to evaluate a unified Grid Operational Risk Score (GORS). Instead of relying on purely data-driven black-box models, we employ a compact single-compartment Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) Spiking Neural Network (SNN) to capture temporal grid dynamics. To encourage operational consistency and logical reliability of the risk assessment, we introduce a differentiable neuro-symbolic rule layer that translates discrete expert heuristics into continuous boundary targets, alongside a physics-constrained learning layer that penalizes operational consistency violations. Furthermore, we develop an unsupervised closed-loop refinement mechanism that leverages internal consistency residuals-comprising symbolic and physical violations-to dynamically inject corrective feedback currents, reducing dependence on manually annotated risk labels. Experiments on the multi-region PSML dataset show that the proposed framework provides interpretable and structurally consistent risk assessment under renewable and weather-induced uncertainty, highlighting a trade-off between predictive fitting accuracy and operational reliability.

title: AI-Driven Agent-Based Urban Digital Twins: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) and agent-based approaches to support intelligent and autonomous urban systems. However, existing reviews largely examine DTs, AI techniques, or agent-based approaches separately, leaving limited insight into how these dimensions interact and how such systems progress toward higher levels of intelligence and real-world deployment. This systematic literature review (SLR) analyzes 82 primary research studies describing AI-driven agent-based approaches in urban digital twins as a system of systems and found in four major scientific databases, i.e. IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library. The selected studies were systematically examined with respect to digital twin types, AI techniques used, agent type, agent roles, maturity level, application domains, and key challenges. As a result, we categorize digital twins into five types: conceptual DT, descriptive DT, predictive DT, prescriptive DT and autonomous DT, with the most frequent being the predictive DT. Reinforcement learning emerged as the most common AI technique, while the hierarchical agent taxonomy shows that multi-agent systems dominate at the architectural level, and decision-making and acting is the main role of agents, followed by control. We also identified that most studies remain at relatively low Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) and rely predominantly on simulation-based or conceptual validation, revealing a substantial gap between technological advancement and real-world deployment. The analysis further shows that implementation challenges evolve across the DT life-cycle. Moreover, we found that only a limited proportion of studies explicitly address uncertainty, while the majority rely on deterministic or idealized assumptions. Our analysis further revealed that most urban digital twin systems are in the early stages of development, and we identified key research gaps and, based on this, suggested future research directions. Overall, this SLR provides a structured synthesis of AI-driven agent-based urban digital twins and identifies priorities for interoperability, standardized evaluation, real-world validation, and scalable autonomous urban systems.

title: Harmonic Signature-Based User Profiling in Smart Grids: A Multi-Feature Fusion Framework Integrating Load Patterns and Spectral Distortion Characteristics
abstract: The growing intrusion of nonlinear load in smart grids has brought more pressure to identify sophisticated methods of user profiling that take it beyond the traditional load-based profiling. The present research will explore ways of developing and verifying a harmonic signature user profiling system through a combination of spectral distortion features with electricity load patterns. The quantitative research approach was chosen, whereby a Python-level analytical pipeline consisting of data simulation, raw data processing, dimensionality reduction, feature fusion, and supervised learning with several classifiers was implemented. These findings indicate that there is a clear distinction between residential, commercial, and industrial users, with average load and total harmonic distortion (THD) showing a different cluster structure. Classification performance was also good with a random forest model having 94.67% accuracy and Logistic Regression with 98.67% accuracy, and respective of the confusion matrices. The paper finds that load and harmonic include features that significantly increase the accuracy of user profiling in intelligent grid systems. Future research is advised to implement the framework on smart meter experiments in the real world. In practice, the strategy helps to better segment consumers and manage the utility demand side. One of the main drawbacks is the use of simulated information instead of real operational measurements.

title: Intelligent control and optimization of power system facilities using artificial neural networks
venue: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: As electric power systems modernize, the need to develop intelligent decision support methods for the technical refurbishment and reconstruction of electrical grid facilities is increasing. This study aims to develop an intelligent approach to selecting priority alternatives for modernizing power grid facilities based on artificial neural networks (ANN). This paper proposes a two-level decision-making structure: a tactical level for selecting preferred alternatives for individual power grid facilities, and a strategic level for setting modernization priorities at the regional power grid level. To evaluate alternatives, a system of specific criteria was developed, encompassing economic, technical, reliability, and socio-environmental indicators. A new criterion for unifying equipment nomenclature is proposed, enabling the classification of technical solutions and the clustering of alternatives using Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOM). A multilayer neural network trained with backpropagation was employed to evaluate alternative preferences. Experimental studies have shown that the best results are achieved with the Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) algorithm and a three-layer network architecture, yielding an F-score of up to 0.979 and a classification accuracy of 99.04%. The results confirm the effectiveness of neural network methods for intelligent decision support in modernizing the electric power infrastructure.

title: A Survey of Rainfall-Induced Challenges on Authentication Mechanisms in IoT-Enabled Solar Photovoltaic Networks
venue: International Conference on Innovation & Growth in Next-Gen Intelligent Technology & Engineering (IGNITE)
abstract: To have safe monitoring and control of distributed energy resources, the solar photovoltaic (PV) systems powered by the Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices require good wireless communication and powerful authentication protocols. Many environmental factors may influence wireless communication. When it pours, the quality of the wireless channel and the effectiveness of the authentication protocols particularly with outdoor deployment deteriorates mostly. The paper examines the previous literature that investigated the impact of rain on the quality of wireless links in solar IoT networks. The studies all indicate that the connection is no longer trusted with poor rain diluting the signal. It results in reduced rates of authentication success and increased delays in handshakes. They also demonstrate that fixed (static) authentication techniques malfunction more frequently and demand more time during downpour in the middle of the rainy season than during typical weather conditions. This review establishes that the ratio of packet delivery (PDR) decreases, handshake latency increases and authentication failures are twice in case of static setups when the rainfall rate is more than 10 mm/h. Policies of adaptive authentication to reduce timeouts, retry count, and backoff steps based on the state of the link or rain can reduce failure rates by 35-50% without negatively impacting clear weather performance. These findings indicate that the most significant issue that should be considered when establishing safe and resilient solar IoT networks is rainfall.

title: Multi-Service Isolation Scheduling for HPLC+HRF Dual-Channel Communication in Low-Voltage Distributed PV Control Networks
venue: International Conference on Electronic Electrical Engineering and Automatic Control (EEEAC)
abstract: The large-scale integration of distributed photovoltaic (PV) units in low-voltage distribution networks introduces heterogeneous communication services, including status acquisition, control command delivery, execution feedback, and maintenance messages. These services have different latency and reliability requirements, but they are often carried over shared local communication resources, which may cause delay fluctuation and feedback collisions when acquisition traffic becomes heavy. To address this problem, this paper proposes a multi-service isolation scheduling method for HPLC+HRF dual-channel communication in low-voltage distributed PV control networks. First, a service isolation identifier is designed to map different service classes to differentiated queues, link identifiers, channel modes, and time-slot resources. Then, a priority-aware scheduling weight is introduced to allocate isolated control slots according to service importance, delay constraint, queue length, and retransmission status. To avoid the direct linear weighting of heterogeneous channel indicators, a normalized weighted-product channel evaluation model is adopted for HPLC/HRF channel selection. Moreover, an adaptive time-slot reallocation mechanism is developed to adjust control and feedback resources according to real-time queue state, traffic arrivals, retransmission rate, and deadline pressure. A statistical HPLC+HRF channel model considering HPLC frequency-selective fading, impulsive noise, impedance variation, and HRF wireless fading is incorporated into the discrete-event simulator. Simulation results show that the proposed method effectively reduces average and tail control-service delay, improves deadline satisfaction, and substantially reduces feedback collisions compared with FIFO, priority-based, and non-isolated dual-channel scheduling schemes.

title: AI-Driven Adaptive Smart Grid for Real-Time Energy Optimization and Fault Detection
venue: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering
abstract: Abstract: Conventional smart-grid systems often rely on fixed control strategies that have limited ability to respond dynamically to changing electricity demand, renewable-energy variability, equipment degradation, and unexpected faults. This study proposes an AI-Driven Adaptive Smart Grid (AI-ASG) for real-time energy optimization and automated fault detection. The framework integrates machine learning, real-time sensing, adaptive demand-response control, and intelligent fault classification to improve grid efficiency, reliability, and operational responsiveness. A mixed-methods quantitative and qualitative research design was adopted. Smart-grid operational data, including load demand, voltage, current, frequency, power factor, renewable-energy generation, and equipment-fault indicators, were processed through preprocessing, feature extraction, and AI-based prediction. Adaptive optimization was evaluated using energy consumption reduction, peak-load reduction, renewable-energy utilization, power-loss reduction, voltage stability, fault-detection accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, false-alarm rate, detection latency, computational overhead, and system scalability. Qualitative assessment considered interpretability, operator usability, interoperability, adaptability, and decision-support effectiveness. Performance was compared with conventional rule-based control, non-adaptive machine-learning control, and the proposed adaptive AI approach. The proposed AI-ASG demonstrated improved operational performance across energy-management and fault-detection measures. Quantitative evaluation indicated reductions in unnecessary energy consumption and peak demand, improved renewable-energy utilization and voltage stability, and faster fault identification. The adaptive model also achieved higher fault-classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score while reducing false alarms and detection latency compared with conventional approaches. Qualitative findings indicated improved system interpretability, operator confidence, adaptability, and real-time decision support. The proposed AI-driven adaptive architecture provides an integrated approach for intelligent energy optimization and real-time fault management, supporting more responsive, reliable, efficient, and scalable smart-grid operation. title: Penerapan Generative AI dan Building Information Modeling (BIM) dalam Efisiensi Alur Kerja Desain Arsitektur Tropis
abstract: The increasing demand for efficient and climate-responsive building design has encouraged the adoption of digital technologies in architectural practice. However, conventional design workflows often require lengthy iterations due to the separation of creative exploration and technical validation. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and Building Information Modeling (BIM) in improving the efficiency of tropical architectural design while maintaining geometric accuracy and thermal performance. An experimental comparative approach was applied to a five-story office building in Jakarta, Indonesia. The workflow integrated AI-based design generation, BIM-based parametric modeling, interoperability assessment, clash detection, and thermal performance evaluation using the Overall Thermal Transfer Value (OTTV) method. The results show that the proposed AI-BIM workflow reduced design duration from 90.0 to 17.0 hours, achieving an efficiency rate of 81.11%. The average geometry interoperability error was 3.28%, while the selected kinetic façade achieved an OTTV value of 31.22 W/m², satisfying SNI 6389:2020 requirements. Expert validation also indicated high feasibility, with average scores above 4.00 on a five-point Likert scale. The novelty of this study lies in the development of a standardized workflow that transforms AI-generated visual assets into engineering-valid BIM parametric objects for tropical architecture. The findings demonstrate that AI-BIM integration can significantly enhance design productivity, thermal performance, and practical implementation in the construction industry.

title: Energy Security and Sustainability in the GCC : The Conditional and Contested Role of AI and Digital Infrastructure
abstract: ABSTRACT As Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies pursue simultaneous commitments to national AI strategies, renewable energy targets, and Paris Agreement pledges, a key sustainable‐management question remains empirically unresolved: does digital and AI investment genuinely advance energy security and environmental sustainability in hydrocarbon‐dependent economies, or does its contribution depend on institutional conditions policymakers can shape? This study provides a second‐generation panel econometric answer, analyzing all six GCC states from 1996 to 2023 ( N = 168). Three contributions distinguish this work: we separate digital infrastructure (DII) from AI‐specific deployment (ADI) as econometrically distinct constructs; we introduce the Climate Stress Index (CSI), extending environmental assessment beyond CO 2 accounting to vulnerability and disaster exposure; and, using estimators suited to a small, cross‐sectionally dependent panel (CCEMG, AMG) alongside country‐level, leave‐one‐out, placebo, and cross‐validated machine‐learning checks, we show energy efficiency and hydrocarbon revenue dependence, not digitalization per se, are the most robust levers of GCC energy security, a result validated against a placebo null distribution and corroborated by independent machine‐learning rankings. Digital infrastructure and AI deployment show smaller, estimator‐sensitive, and governance‐conditional associations; we report this conditionality transparently rather than overstating a still‐emerging relationship. Governance quality is the strongest Granger‐causal driver of energy security in the panel. For sustainable management practice, the findings reframe GCC digital strategy: AI investment should be sequenced alongside, not as a substitute for, energy‐efficiency policy, revenue diversification, and governance strengthening. We provide quantified policy guidance for GCC governments and a transparent, replicable template for evaluating digital‐sustainability claims in other resource‐dependent, small‐N‐panel economies.

title: PROSPECTS FOR THE USE OF ENERGY-EFFICIENT TECHNOLOGIES AND ALTERNATIVE ENERGY SOURCES IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF SMART CITIES
venue: Ethiopian International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the prospects for energy-efficient technologies and alternative energy sources used in the construction of modern smart cities. Six categories of solutions are examined in detail: Smart Grid infrastructure, Internet of Things (IoT) systems, intelligent lighting and HVAC technologies, building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV), bioenergy from municipal waste, and geothermal heat pumps. Quantitative analysis based on data from leading smart cities (Copenhagen, Stockholm, Singapore, Vienna, Helsinki, Seoul, Amsterdam) demonstrates that the implementation of Smart Grid technology reduces urban electricity losses by 8–12 %, IoT-based building management systems decrease total energy consumption by 20–30 %, intelligent lighting cuts energy use by 55–65 %, and AI-driven HVAC systems achieve 28–35 % savings. Integrated alternative energy sources can cover up to 35–50 % of a city's energy balance, with the leading smart cities currently achieving 42–73 % renewable energy share in their total mix. The combined deployment of these technologies enables a 30–55 % reduction in CO₂ emissions.
