title: DIGITAL TWIN-BASED SMART GRID MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE POWER INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT IN SAUDI ARABIA
abstract: The power industry in Saudi Arabia is undergoing a transformation from a system in which electricity is centrally dispatched and which is based mainly on hydrocarbons to one that is more varied and incorporates utility-scale renewable energy, distributed resources, storage, digital substations, and control systems that demand ever-increasing amounts of data. This change brings with it a management problem because merely expanding the physical grid is not sufficient to guarantee the continuous monitoring, predictive capabilities, coordination between various assets, and the ability to learn over the lifetime that are necessary in a network with a high proportion of renewables. The article examines digital twin technology as a means of managing the sustainable development of power infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. It carries out a systematic and integrated review of peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2025, drawing on evidence from the fields of digital twin architecture, smart-grid operation, renewable energy integration, microgrids, edge intelligence, cybersecurity, asset management, and studies of Saudi Arabias energy transition. The review distinguishes between monitoring replicas and operational twins that are capable of achieving state synchronization, forecasting, scenario testing, and controlled feedback.

title: Formation of structural model of objects of power systems on the basis of artificial neural networks
venue: IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The article presents an approach to optimizing the processes of the technical re-equipment and reconstruction (TRR) of power grid facilities using artificial neural networks (ANN). A two-level decision-making structure is proposed, including the tactical level (selection of preferred alternatives for individual facilities) and the strategic level (prioritization for the regional power system or RPS). Mathematical models of private criteria have been developed to evaluate alternatives: economic costs, technical efficiency, reliability, socio-ecological consequences, and equipment unification. The concept of “nomenclature unification criterion” was introduced, which allows clustering of solutions based on the typing of equipment parameters. Training of neural networks was carried out using the algorithm of error back propagation, which provided high accuracy of classification of alternatives (F-measure up to 0.979). Experiments showed the effectiveness of the Levenberg-Marquardt method for training networks with three hidden layers. The integration of ANN into automated decision support systems (ADSS) allows minimizing subjective factors, increasing the adaptability of power systems to changing conditions, and optimizing resource allocation. Results demonstrate the ability to reduce risks and improve infrastructure reliability by processing noisy and incomplete data, as well as real-time analysis. The approach applies to large-scale power systems, balancing short-term and long-term modernization goals.

title: Decision Fusion of Classification and Forecasting for Electricity Theft Detection in Smart Grids
venue: IEEE International Conference on Advanced Power Engineering and Energy (APEE)
abstract: Existing machine learning approaches for electricity theft detection (ETD) primarily focus on improving classification performance but often generate excessive false alarms, increasing inspection costs and reducing operational efficiency in smart grids. This paper presents a decision-level cross-verification framework that combines structural classification with independent temporal anomaly verification to support confidence-based inspection prioritization. The proposed approach employs an optimized stacking ensemble classifier for structural theft detection together with a NeuralProphet-based forecasting module that identifies temporal anomalies using residual-based indicators and percentile-based thresholds. The proposed AND-based decision-level fusion strategy integrates the outputs of both analytical modules to identify high-confidence theft cases supported by complementary structural and temporal evidence. Experimental evaluation on the SGCC benchmark dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed cross-verification strategy. Compared with the standalone structural classifier, the proposed cross-verification strategy reduces false positives by approximately 45% while maintaining high precision (93.08%) for inspection-oriented decision support. Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical approach for high-confidence inspection prioritization in smart grid environments.

title: ESP32-Based Three-Phase IoT Energy Meter with Accuracy Analysis Under Nonlinear Load Conditions
abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and experimental validation of a compact three-phase electrical energy meter, the TriPhase Smart Node (TSN), based on an ESP32 microcontroller and the dedicated ATM90E32 energy-metering integrated circuit. The proposed device measures voltage, current, active, reactive, and apparent power, power factor, and frequency in a three-phase system, while providing native MQTT connectivity and relay-based load control. Baseline measurement accuracy was quantified against a certified PQ BOX 150 power quality analyzer under five controlled load conditions, including non-linear current profiles with current crest factors from 1.41 to 5. The pre-calibration results show voltage measurement deviations up to 0.81 %, current deviations up to 1.91 %, and active power deviations up to 2.17 %. These deviations identify systematic gain and phase-error components in the analog measurement chain and motivate subsequent ATM90E32 register calibration. The paper further identifies a systematic limitation of reactive power measurement under distorted waveforms, caused by the absence of distortion power evaluation in the metering IC.

title: A review of distributed generation technologies and their impact on modern power systems
venue: Journal of Electrical Systems and Information Technology
abstract: Abstract Globally, there is a significant transformation involving conventional power systems, such transformations are driven by concerns over climate change, energy security, and sustainability. In recent decades, more distributed generation (DG) systems and distributed energy resources (DER) systems have penetrated the conventional power grids, particularly those based on wind and solar technologies. The rapid technological developments of DER systems are largely governed by advancements in power electronics technologies and related fields, which form the core of the characteristics of modern power systems. However, the increasing relevance of DER systems has transformed traditional unidirectional power flow into bidirectional power flow, introducing new challenges to system stability, reliability, and security. As a result, various international standards, grid codes (GCs), and inverter control algorithms that shape key power systems parameters; such as active power/ frequency control (APC/F C ) and reactive power/voltage control (RPC/V C ), are evolving. In addition, emerging concept known as fault ride-through (FRT) capabilities together with modern power electronics-based protection logics are been developed to facilitate secure and reliable integration of DER into modern power grids. The paper reviews the key technical, regulatory, and policy challenges associated with DER integration, including issues related to control algorithms, grid interoperability, and operational flexibility. Furthermore, it presents an overview of power systems supportive functions provided by DER inverters, which are categorized into reactive power/voltage control (RPC), voltage ride-through (VRT), and frequency ride-through (FRT) capabilities. The advantages, limitations, and evolution of these control algorithms and research gaps in both policy challenges and technical challenges are analyzed, along with emerging trends that will continue to shape the future of modern power systems.

title: AI-Optimized Energy-Efficient Multi-Band Wireless Sensor Networks for Real-Time Monitoring and Resilient Communication in U.S. Smart Grid Infrastructure
venue: American Journal of Advanced Technology and Engineering Solutions
abstract: Reliable real-time monitoring in United States smart grid infrastructure is challenged by spectrum interference, limited sensor energy, communication delays, and disruptions across heterogeneous wireless sensor networks. This study examines the relationships between artificial intelligence (AI) optimization capabilities and energy efficiency, real-time monitoring performance, and communication resilience in multi-band wireless sensor networks. Guided by Complex Adaptive Systems Theory, it adopts a quantitative, explanatory, cross-sectional, embedded multiple-case design focused on advanced metering, distribution automation, smart substations, distributed energy resource monitoring, and utility communication systems. Criterion-based purposive sampling targets network engineers, smart grid specialists, utility communications personnel, reliability professionals, and technical managers across 18 infrastructure cases, with 320 respondents specified for the study. A structured five-point Likert questionnaire assesses adaptive multi-band spectrum optimization, sensor energy and duty-cycle management, and predictive routing and network recovery as explanatory variables, alongside three perceived network performance outcomes. The analytical framework combines descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression with deployment-level adjustments to evaluate nine directional hypotheses. The manuscript reports mean scores of 3.79 for energy efficiency, 3.68 for monitoring performance, and 3.75 for communication resilience, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from .82 to .90. Predictor-outcome correlations range from r = .36 to .64. Regression models report explained variance of 51.6%, 54.4%, and 60.0% for energy efficiency, monitoring performance, and resilience, respectively. The strongest standardized relationships involve sensor energy management and energy efficiency (β = .39), spectrum optimization and monitoring performance (β = .34), and predictive routing and communication resilience (β = .42), with reported significance at p < .05 across nine associations. The framework highlights the value of coordinating spectrum allocation, energy-aware scheduling, and automated recovery within utility networks, and supports structured evaluation of performance, reliability, and operational adaptability across diverse smart grid deployments, while recognizing that cross-sectional associations cannot establish causal effects.

title: 6G-Enabled Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Intelligent Vehicle-to-Grid Energy Optimization and Renewable Integration in Smart Grids: A Data-Driven Analytics Framework and Simulation Study
abstract: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) coordination asks hundreds of charging hubs to decide, every few minutes, how much to charge or discharge the vehicles connected to them so that energy cost, peak demand, transformer loading, battery wear and users' departure needs are balanced while renewable generation is absorbed. Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MARL) is a natural control architecture for this problem, and sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems promise the ultra-reliable low-latency links and edge intelligence it needs, but the value of that connectivity has rarely been quantified. This article designs a data-driven analytics framework that links a physical feeder-and-fleet model, a communication layer, a multi-agent learning layer and a decision layer, and evaluates it on a transparent simulation testbed: a radial feeder with eight charging hubs and 200 vehicles behind a 1,200 kW transformer, hub-level photovoltaics and feeder-level wind, duck-curve prices and carbon intensity, and three communication archetypes (4G-LTE, 5G, 6G) that differ in message loss, setpoint delay, fleet-flexibility messaging and eligibility for fast reserve products. Five policies are compared on 40 held-out days: uncontrolled charging, a time-of-use heuristic, independent deep Q-learning, value-decomposition MARL and a perfect-information linear-programming bound. Every coordinated policy removed the transformer overload of uncontrolled charging, cutting daily cost by 27–40%; the learned policies beat a capacity-aware heuristic only when the network supplied fleet-flexibility messages and reserve eligibility (by 2.5–7.8% under 6G, not under 4G) while remaining 30–41% above the bound. The value of 6G over 4G to the learned policy was 613 per vehicle-year gross and 552 net of a connectivity premium, positive in every economic draw, split between a market channel (reserve eligibility) and an information channel (fleet messages), with link loss and delay worth little and the reserve price explaining 87% of its variance. Savings rose with photovoltaics and price volatility, and the policy did not generalise to a feeder without photovoltaics. All inputs are stylised with stated ranges; the testbed and results file are provided.

title: Digital twin-assisted edge-local query resolution for privacy–utility trade-off in location-based services
abstract: Location-Based Services (LBS) generate large volumes of sensitive, location-dependent queries that must be processed under strict and often conflicting constraints of privacy and utility. Existing differential privacy (DP) mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: strong guarantees inject excessive noise and degrade utility, while utility-oriented methods under-protect users. We propose DT-ELR (Digital Twin-assisted Edge-Local Resolution), a framework that jointly optimises disclosure and retrieval utility through two tightly integrated algorithms and an on-device digital twin. Algorithm 1 (SensitivityClassifier) calibrates a monotone geo-indistinguishability budget from a data-derived sensitivity score, validated against a semantic venue-category labelling (AUC 0.81). The digital twin predicts from on-device signals alone whether releasing a query would improve its answer (AUC 0.90); self-sufficient queries are resolved against an on-device venue cache with no release and no budget spent. Algorithm 2 (ClosedFormAllocator) then distributes the remaining budget across released queries in closed form, matching the exact dynamic-programming optimum to within 1%. Experiments on three public check-in corpora - Foursquare-NYC, Gowalla and Brightkite - using an end-to-end nearest-venue retrieval task and three implemented adversaries, show that DT-ELR reduces optimal-inference localization success on sensitive queries from 61.3% to 11.4% on Foursquare-NYC at a matched mean budget, while raising end-to-end retrieval precision from 0.244 under full release to 0.559. Twin-guided release routing outperforms a tuned distance heuristic at every matched release rate, approaching an oracle ceiling of 0.565, and keeps 73% of sensitive queries entirely on the device. Component analysis confirms that each mechanism contributes independently, with edge-local resolution dominant, and the sensitivity model transfers to Gowalla and Brightkite without refitting. Against three recent location-perturbation mechanisms at a matched budget, DT-ELR attains a dominant privacy-utility frontier on all three corpora: higher utility at equal disclosure, and lower disclosure at equal utility.

title: GOVERNING INNOVATION: POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS, BUSINESS STRATEGIES, HEALTHCARE SYSTEMS AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT IN THE ERA OF INTELLIGENT TECHNOLOGIES
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: Globally, smart technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) is proliferating quickly and reshaping political institutions, business practices, healthcare delivery systems, and civil infrastructure development. This review discusses how governments, organizations, health systems, and infrastructure planners are adjusting governance, strategic frameworks, and engineering practices to embrace AI-enabled innovation, while managing risks. We used a narrative review methodology, synthesizing peer-reviewed literature, policy reports, and institutional publications published between 2016 and 2026 obtained from Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases. The review identifies five interconnected themes: (1) The changing role of political institutions in regulating AI through policy frameworks and digital governance initiatives; (2) Business adoption strategies for AI integration, including automation of decision-making and transformation of the workforce; (3) AI applications in healthcare systems, including diagnostics and patient care, along with ethical and equity concerns; (4) Integration of intelligent systems in civil engineering and infrastructure, including smart construction, structural health monitoring, and resilient urban planning; and (5) Broader social implications such as algorithmic bias, labor displacement, and digital inequality. Findings suggest that while intelligent technologies produce significant efficiency and innovation gains across sectors, fragmented regulatory approaches and uneven institutional capacity create governance gaps that are disproportionately borne by vulnerable populations and under-resourced infrastructure systems. The review finds that effective governance of AI requires coordinated multi-stakeholder frameworks that include political oversight, responsible business practices, equitable healthcare policy, and resilient infrastructure planning. Future research should explore comparative cross-national governance models and longitudinal assessments of AI’s socioeconomic and infrastructural impact.

title: An integrated AI-based software architecture for load forecasting, controlled anomaly detection, and predictive energy management
abstract: The increasing deployment of smart meters and Internet of Things technologies has created a demand for intelligent computational systems capable of jointly forecasting electricity consumption, detecting abnormal behavior, and optimizing load management. This study proposes an integrated artificial intelligence-based framework for automated energy metering and consumption management in smart-grid environments. The framework combines a Long Short-Term Memory network for short-term load forecasting, an autoencoder-based model for anomaly detection, and Model Predictive Control for demand-side optimization. The system architecture includes data acquisition, communication, preprocessing, predictive analytics, anomaly monitoring, and decision-support layers. The primary empirical evaluation used 4,380 measured hourly observations (approximately 6 months) from a single administrative building. A separately flagged synthetic temporal extension was retained only as an auxiliary dataset and was excluded from all primary performance metrics. Across five independent model initializations, the final LSTM achieved a MAPE of 3.423 ± 0.555%, an RMSE of 0.336 ± 0.048 kW, and an R 2 of 0.973 ± 0.007 on the 633-sequence independent measured test subset. The synthetic extension was maintained as a separately identified auxiliary component and was excluded from all primary training, validation, and independent test metrics. Using a validation-selected reconstruction-error threshold, the autoencoder detected 12 of 30 controlled anomalies in the independent test subset, yielding 100.00% precision, 40.00% recall, and an F1-score of 57.14%. Under the same controlled protocol, One-Class SVM achieved higher recall (53.33%) and F1-score (69.57%), indicating that the autoencoder should be interpreted as an architectural component rather than as the best-performing anomaly detector for the present dataset. A historical proof-of-concept MPC simulation, retained for architectural illustration, reported a 15% reduction in simulated peak demand and a 12% reduction in estimated electricity cost; these values are not interpreted as measured outcomes from the administrative-building experiment. Controlled anomaly injection was used to establish reproducible validation and test labels for the anomaly-detection component. The results demonstrate that the joint integration of forecasting, anomaly detection, and predictive control provides a computationally coherent framework for supporting energy-management efficiency, operational reliability, and data-driven decision-making in intelligent energy systems.

title: Toward Cybersecure Smart Power Systems: A Review of Vulnerability Assessment Methods and Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection Strategies
venue: IEEE International Conference on Renewable Energy and Sustainable E-Mobility (RESEM)
abstract: Today, power systems are smart, with digital communication, automation and distributed energy resources making the traditional electrical grid into an intelligent smart grid. These developments help to streamline processes, ensure reliability and optimize energy use, but they also raise serious cyber security risks. Smart grids depend on complex networks of sensors, communications, and control that can be a source of cyber vulnerabilities. These attacks can affect the stability of the grid, spoof data available to the operators and result in widespread power blackouts. This study is an extensive survey of vulnerabilities in smart electric power grid and advanced techniques on cyberattack detection and prevention. The paper discusses the most prevalent threats faced by smart grid systems such as False Data Injection (FDI), Denial of Service (DoS) Attacks, Malware Attack, and Communication Protocol Exploitation. Also, recent development of machine learning and deep learning-based detection mechanisms are examined to detect abnormal network behavior and malicious activities in real-time. The study also addresses the concepts of vulnerability assessment frameworks, intrusion detection systems, and resilient grid architectures aimed at improving the cybersecurity measures in intelligent power networks. The paper reviews the recent research trends and technological advances, and identifies effective solutions to enhance the cyber-resilience of next-generation power grid. The results are helpful to enhance secure energy infrastructure that can support reliable and stable electricity supply in increasingly digital energy ecosystems.

title: Differentially Private Release of AC-OPF Benchmarks with Feasibility and Cost Fidelity Guarantees
venue: International Conference on Energy, Power and Electrical Technology (ICEPET)
abstract: The release of realistic optimal power flow (OPF) benchmark cases is fundamental to energy systems research, yet disclosing detailed load data raises serious privacy concerns for industrial and residential consumers. Classical differential privacy (DP) mechanisms address privacy by injecting calibrated random noise into published loads; however, the magnitude of noise required for meaningful privacy guarantees frequently destroys the AC feasibility of the underlying OPF problem, rendering the released benchmark useless for simulation. This paper formulates the Load Indistinguishability (LI) problem, which jointly requires that the released load vector satisfies a formal $(\epsilon, \alpha)$-indistinguishability guarantee and that the OPF solved on the obfuscated loads incurs a dispatch cost within a prescribed fraction $\beta$ of the original optimum. An exact bilevel mechanism (MOLI) satisfying both requirements is developed, together with three computationally tractable approximations: a single-level feasibility relaxation $\left(\mathcal{M}_{R}\right)$, a Fritz-John reformulation $\left(\mathcal{M}_{F J}\right)$, and an iterative Min-Max scheme $\left(\mathcal{M}_{M}\right)$. Theoretical guarantees covering privacy, feasibility, and accuracy are established for each mechanism. Numerical experiments on 29 NESTA benchmark networks confirm that all three mechanisms achieve substantially smaller load distortion than unconstrained Laplace perturbation, and that $\mathcal{M}_{M}$ reliably enforces cost fidelity even at tight tolerance levels.

title: Metaheuristic and Nonlinear Optimization for Intelligent Energy and Environmental Systems: A Review of Renewable Generation, Smart Metering, Networks and Environmental Monitoring
venue: International Journal Of Recent Trends In Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: Energy and environmental systems are full of decisions that must be tuned under uncertainty: how much power to draw from a solar panel, how to bill and balance consumption on a smart grid, how to share spectrum in a wireless network and how to read a biosensor in the field. Computing itself is part of the problem, since data centres, web services and smartphones draw a growing share of electricity. Many of these decisions have no closed-form solution because the underlying models are nonlinear, noisy or only partly known. Metaheuristic search, fuzzy reasoning, nonlinear analysis and data-driven forecasting are now used to find good settings, but studies are spread across power engineering, networking and environmental science. This chapter reviews optimization and learning methods for five groups of problems: renewable generation and grid interfacing, smart metering and energy forecasting, resource allocation and energy-aware computing in communication and IoT systems, environmental and agricultural monitoring, and the approximation of nonlinear physical models. The review finds that hybrid metaheuristics, such as grey wolf optimization with opposition-based learning, improve tracking and control in renewable systems, that tree ensembles and regression models are standard for consumption forecasting, that fuzzy optimization handles uncertainty in network resource allocation, that signal-aware transfer scheduling and green design guidelines reduce the energy used by smartphones and web services, and that neural approximation can stand in for expensive solvers of nonlinear equations. Few studies, however, compare methods on shared benchmarks or report computation cost. Future work should use common test systems, report run time next to solution quality and link optimization with forecasting in one loop.

title: AI-Driven WAMS Framework for Proactive Voltage Stability in EV-Integrated Distribution Networks
venue: IEEE International Conference on Renewable Energy and Sustainable E-Mobility (RESEM)
abstract: High density Electric Vehicles (EVs) put enormous stochastic strain on the distribution system, and leads to critical voltage instability. The paper offers a strong framework by integrating the artificial intelligence (AI) along with the Wide Area Monitoring Systems (WAMS) to ensure that the grid is more resilient. High-frequency synchronized information of Phasor Measurement Unit (PMUs) is used to train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to provide accurate and short-term load forecasting. The APE of the proposed model stands at 1.28 that is lower than the conventional persistence standard. The predictions are used by a real time Voltage Stability Assessment (VSA) module to activate proactive decentralized charging settings. The framework, which has been tested on the IEEE 33-bus system, keeps the voltage profile above 0.95 p.u. in case of spikes in EV charging and decreases the loss of the system by 13.1%. The findings prove that the suggested AI-WAMS architecture is computationally feasible and essential to the safe functioning of the current sustainable power systems.

title: Machine Learning Regression Modeling and Cross-Regional Prediction of Photovoltaic Power Generation
abstract: This study proposes a machine-learning framework for modeling and predicting photovoltaic (PV) power generation across diverse climatic conditions. One year of high-resolution operational data from a grid-connected PV system, including solar irradiation, ambient temperature, and wind speed, is used to train regression models for power prediction. Multiple techniques, such as Gaussian process regression, artificial neural networks, decision trees, and support vector methods, along with their variants, are evaluated to determine the most accurate and robust approach. Results indicate that the squared exponential Gaussian process model provides the best predictive performance and generalization. To extend applicability beyond a single site, the study introduces a cross-regional prediction strategy that applies the trained model to meteorological datasets from nine geographically distinct cities. This enables data-driven estimation of PV generation potential in locations without measured PV output, offering a scalable alternative to conventional site assessments. SHAP and partial-dependence analyses provide interpretability, confirming solar irradiation as the dominant driver, with temperature and wind contributing secondary effects. The framework demonstrates physically consistent cross-regional predictions and shows potential for preliminary renewable-energy assessment and planning.

title: Transition to Renewable Energy: Pathways Toward a Sustainable, Reliable, And Low-Carbon Energy System
abstract: The transition to renewable electricity presents U.S. utilities with a persistent challenge: reducing carbon emissions while preserving dependable supply and managing investment costs. This study examines how renewable integration and complementary technological and institutional capabilities relate to decarbonization, reliability, and affordability. Guided by the Energy Trilemma Framework, it adopts a quantitative, explanatory, cross-sectional, embedded multiple-case design involving a proposed sample of 300 energy professionals across 24 U.S. electric utility cases. Purposive sampling and a five-point Likert questionnaire assess renewable integration maturity, energy storage and grid flexibility, grid modernization, demand-side management, and regulatory and financial support. Outcome variables comprise perceived carbon reduction, electricity reliability, and transition affordability. The analytical plan combines descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and interaction-based moderation, with organizational controls and utility-level electricity and emissions benchmarks. The manuscript reports mean scores of 3.94 for carbon reduction, 3.82 for reliability, and 3.57 for affordability, with reliability coefficients ranging from .81 to .90. Renewable integration correlates positively with carbon reduction (r = .58; β = .46), while storage flexibility (β = .31), grid modernization (β = .24), and demand management (β = .18) are positively associated with reliability. Regulatory and financial support is associated with integration maturity (β = .42) and affordability (β = .33). The integration-by-flexibility interaction is positive (β = .15, p = .012), and the respective models report explained variance of 39% for carbon reduction, 47% for reliability, 32% for integration, and 27% for affordability. The proposed case-level comparisons distinguish professional perceptions from independent generation, interruption, and emissions records, strengthening interpretation across diverse American utilities. All seven specified relationships meet the manuscript's p < .05 criterion. These patterns emphasize coordinated renewable deployment, storage, responsive demand, modernized grids, and predictable financing as priorities for evaluating balanced utility energy transitions, without establishing causal or verified operational improvements.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection of Smart Meter Electricity Consumption Data
venue: IEEE International Conference on Renewable Energy and Sustainable E-Mobility (RESEM)
abstract: The high-resolution monitoring of electricity consumption achieved through the extensive implementation of smart meters with the advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) has been used to characterize the unlabeled, heterogeneous, and hard-to-analyze data. The paper gives a comparative unsupervised anomaly detection system of residential smart meter data gathered in Bareilly, India, which consists of more than one million measurements that are taken at a time interval of three minutes. Three unsupervised algorithms namely Isolation Forest (IF), Local Outlier Factor (LOF), and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), on smart meter electricity consumption data have been applied. Findings reveal the superiority of IF in detecting the extreme current anomalies (Cohen's d=4.677), while LOF excels in identifying the subtle deviations (Cohen's d=0.494). Meanwhile, PCA is found much faster but has an average “Cohen's d score” PCA had moderate separability (average Cohen's d=1.570). The ensemble model also demonstrated strong detection of anomalies with or combination of any two (IF & LOF or LOF & PCA or IF& PCA or combination of all three. Temporal analysis highlights critical anomaly spikes, particularly between 6 am and 8 am. These findings offer actionable insights for deploying robust and context-aware anomaly detection systems in dynamic smart grid environments.

title: A clustering-based framework to analyse intra-building variability in residential energy performance using geometric descriptors
abstract: Understanding variability in residential energy performance at dwelling level remains challenging due to the combined influence of physical characteristics, occupant-related factors and data privacy constraints. This study uses a demonstrator building to propose clustering-based methodological framework to analyse intra-building variability while preserving data anonymity. Dwelling typologies are defined exclusively using geometric and solar exposure descriptors, avoiding the inclusion of energy variables and preventing feedback between classification and evaluation. Energy performance is subsequently assessed using Weather-Normalised Heating Energy Intensity and Degree-Hours of Discomfort analysed at daily resolution and aggregated at monthly and interannual scales. The methodology is demonstrated through its application to a social housing building over three consecutive winter seasons. Results reveal differentiated patterns of energy use across typologies, which remain consistent in their relative behaviour over time despite seasonal variations in magnitude. However, a substantial level of variability is observed within clusters, indicating that similar geometric configurations can be associated with markedly different energy performance outcomes. In contrast, thermal deficit remains generally low and appears as intermittent events, with no consistent relationship to the geometric descriptors considered. The combined analysis highlights a partial decoupling between energy use and indoor thermal conditions, indicating that energy consumption alone does not fully represent indoor performance. From a methodological perspective, the proposed framework enables the identification of useful typological patterns for several stakeholders while supporting privacy-aware analysis through cluster-based aggregation. The approach provides a methodological basis for analysing residential energy performance in privacy-sensitive contexts and supports the detection of atypical behaviour at building scale.

title: Machine Learning for Solar Radiation and Photovoltaic Systems: Evidence, Validation, and Operational Applications
abstract: Machine learning is used in solar-energy forecasting and management, but reported gains depend on the task, data and evaluation design. This review combines descriptive Scopus bibliometric mapping with a critical narrative synthesis of applications in irradiance estimation, photovoltaic power prediction, fault diagnosis, energy management and grid integration. The photovoltaic search yielded 1,954 unique records published between 2010 and 2026; a separate solar-energy search returned 6,767 results. Their VOSviewer maps are interpreted independently. We examine technical studies by prediction target, forecast horizon, input data, climate, validation method, benchmark and operational purpose. Results from different sites, targets and test designs cannot establish a universal ranking of model families. Classical, ensemble and deep-learning methods each have useful applications, but their reported accuracy should be interpreted against appropriate baselines and leakage-free temporal tests. External-site evaluation and calibrated uncertainty are essential when forecasts inform operational decisions. Physics-guided approaches may improve consistency, whereas digital twins, graph learning, federated learning and autonomous control require more task-specific validation. The review identifies transparent search reporting, reproducible data processing and cross-climate testing as priorities. Because the complete search history and technical screening records are unavailable, the synthesis is descriptive rather than systematic, and bibliometric counts do not measure model quality.

title: AI-Based Electricity Theft Detection System: A Comparative Performance Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models
abstract: Electricity theft is a worldwide challenge that causes significant losses for utility companies, with annual revenue losses estimated at USD 89.3 billion globally. The widespread rollout of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and smart meters has made it easier to access large amounts of high-frequency consumption data from consumers. This access allows companies to use data-driven strategies for electricity theft detection. This review looks at how well machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models detect electricity theft (ETD) using three benchmark datasets. The datasets presented are the State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC) dataset, the Open Energy Data Initiative Theft Detection Dataset 2022 (OEDI/TDD2022), and the Irish Commission for Energy Regulation Smart Metering Project (CER SMP) dataset. A thorough evaluation of 27 models is conducted, covering classical machine learning classifiers, tree ensemble methods, anomaly detection techniques, recurrent neural networks, convolutional networks, Transformer-based encoders, and federated learning systems. Key preprocessing methods, including filling in missing values, normalization, feature engineering, and tackling class imbalance with SMOTE and LoRAS, are noted for each model. The findings show that deep learning methods consistently outperform traditional machine learning techniques across all three benchmark datasets. The CNN-LSTM model, improved with LoRAS, achieves the top reported F1-score of 97.7% on the SGCC dataset. Meanwhile, the Federated ConvGRU model reaches the highest accuracy of 97.8% on OEDI/TDD2022. Transformer architectures show the best overall performance in average categories, with a mean accuracy of 95.8% and a mean F1-score of 95.5%. Addressing class imbalance is seen as the most influential factor, showing an 18.7 percentage-point difference in F1 scores between unaugmented and augmented LSTM models on SGCC. This review concludes that combining hybrid augmentation-driven deep learning architectures with privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks offers the most scalable and practical way to design Electricity theft detection (ETD) systems. The research community should prioritize standardized cross-dataset benchmarking and mandatory reporting of computational complexity as immediate priorities.

title: An artificial intelligence based framework for smart power grid management using an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub with multimodal document processing
abstract: The growing sophistication and need to have sustainable energy systems has led to the shift of the conventional power grids to smart power grids. Such grids are equipped with innovative technologies that include digital communication, Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to increase the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of energy delivery. This paper introduce an AI-based approach to smart power grid management, with the emphasis on the incorporation of an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub that would be able to process multimodal data, such as textual reports, images, videos, and sensor data. The framework applies AI methods of machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics to optimize energy allocation, faults, and failure prediction with minimum human intervention. With real-time analysis, the system dynamically changes the operation of the grids with incoming data, enhancing energy efficiency and lowering the cost of operations by up to 30 percent, between $12,000 and 8,400 in the example of energy optimization. Also, the fault detection system shows a remarkable accuracy of 0.97 in terms of AUC whereas the predictive maintenance model reports an accuracy rate of 95.5. The balancing nature of the energy demand and generation provided by the framework is critical in integrating renewable energy sources since it can help in countering the problem of intermittency of the solar and wind energy. Moreover, the system has a multimodal document processing feature that increases decision-making through the synthesis of various types of data and provides a more detailed overview of grid work. This paper explains how the suggested AI-based framework can greatly improve the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of smart power grids, which will result in the future improvements in energy management.

title: The Role of Institutional Influence in Boosting Smart Meter Acceptance: A Study Using Extended UTAUT2 in Indonesia
venue: Australasian Accounting Business and Finance Journal
abstract: Smart meters are a vital technology for enhancing electrical grid efficiency within intelligent grid systems, yet consumer acceptance continues to limit their full potential. This study addresses the research gap in understanding smart meter adoption in Indonesia by applying an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) model, modified to include institutional influence as a significant factor. Data was gathered through a survey of 410 individuals and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings highlight that institutional influence is the strongest driver of adoption intention (path coefficient of 0.44), followed by social influence (0.17) and effort expectancy (0.09). Interestingly, performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, and price value did not exhibit significant relationships, suggesting that functional benefits or cost savings are not primary motivators for consumers. These results emphasize the critical role of government policies, regulations, incentives, and educational support in building consumer trust, while also underscoring the importance of user-friendly smart meter designs. Leveraging social encouragement from public figures and community leaders is also recommended to boost adoption rates. Future research could explore the long-term impact of these institutional interventions and examine cultural influences on technology acceptance. Overall, cultivating strong institutional frameworks and supportive social ecosystems is essential for the successful deployment of smart infrastructure in Indonesia, providing key insights for policymakers and practitioners seeking to foster sustainable energy adoption.

title: Mining in the Southern Ecuadorian Amazon: Territorial Transformation and Biodiversity Loss in the Zamora and Nangaritza Rivers
venue: IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)
abstract: The Ecuadorian Amazon faces multiple environmental pressures derived from human activities such as agricultural expansion, infrastructure construction, and oil and mining exploitation. Mining activities induce rapid territorial transformation, compromising the biodiversity and hydrological dynamics of rivers. This study aims to evaluate the impact of mining spatial dynamics through Sentinel-2 imagery and geospatial analysis to identify affected areas in the Zamora and Nangaritza rivers. The methodology was divided into three stages: i) acquisition and processing of satellite images, ii) supervised classification using the Random Forest algorithm, and iii) identification of hotspots through Kernel density maps. The results revealed a 2.22% increase in mining activity, with the greatest losses occurring in the grassland class. Kernel density analysis identified a transformation from three nuclei (2019) to a continuous corridor of high concentration of mining activities in 2024. These findings provide critical information for the implementation of control and monitoring policies for activities of mining in the region.

title: Proof-of-Concept Optimisation of Low-Carbon Power System Dispatch: Assessing the Impact of Doubling Battery Storage Capacity on Operating Cost, Emissions, and Supply Adequacy
abstract: This paper presents a proof-of-concept economic dispatch optimisation model to evaluate the operational, economic, and environmental impacts of scaling Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) within a carbon-constrained power network. Four distinct scenarios are evaluated over a deterministic 24-hour horizon: Baseline, Flexible, Low-carbon, and Doubled-Storage (120 MWh). The simulation results reveal a profound systemic bottleneck: while enforcing a strict carbon emission cap of 250 tCO2/day successfully reduces environmental impacts by 22%, it triggers severe supply inadequacy. This causes unserved load penalties that escalate daily operating costs from £0.1M to £2.1M. Crucially, doubling the BESS capacity provides zero operational relief, with the storage system remaining completely unutilized and flatlined at its initial state-of-charge. This paper demonstrates that expanding energy storage capacity in isolation—without concurrent over-provisioning of variable renewable generation capacity or dynamic charging architectures—creates a stranded asset that cannot mitigate supply deficits or lower system costs. The findings offer critical cautionary insights for grid planners and policymakers targeting decarbonisation milestones.

title: Applications of Analytics in Delivery: A Bibliometric Study, 2014-2026

abstract: Analytics now shapes how hospitals treat patients, how medicines reach the right cells, and how parcels, power and online courses reach their users. This study maps the research that links delivery and analytics. We searched the Scopus database with the query "Delivery AND Analytics" and, after screening, kept 2,802 journal documents (2,195 articles and 607 reviews) published between 2014 and 2027. Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer were used to study publication and citation trends, leading authors, sources and countries, and the keyword structure of the field. Output grew from 52 papers in 2014 to 544 in 2026, about 21.6 per cent a year, and 2025 and 2026 together hold 38.4 per cent of all documents. Health care dominates: about six in ten documents deal with patients, hospitals or clinical care, and "health care delivery" is the most frequent subject term once generic indexing labels are set aside. The keyword maps show four groups: health-care delivery and management, analytics methods and digital technology, clinical study terms, and drug delivery with precision medicine. Logistics and last-mile delivery form a smaller strand that is growing quickly. The paper also reports the limits of the data. The export has no cited references, so co-citation and bibliographic coupling could not be run, and the word "delivery" covers very different subjects, such as parcel routing and nanoparticle drug carriers.

title: AI-Based IoT Framework for Renewable Energy Forecasting in Smart Grids
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Computing and Sustainable Innovations in Technology (IC-SIT)
abstract: Proper forecasting of renewable energy is critical to the stable and efficient performance of the contemporary smart grids with a high proportion of distributed energy resources. Nonetheless, the nature of intermittency of renewable resources and the heavy use of heterogeneous sensors creates much uncertainty and complexity in prediction models. In this paper, the authors describe an AI-based IoT-driven forecasting model that is aimed to enhance short-term forecasting in renewable energy in smart grids. The offered solution combines real-time IoT data streaming with an edge-cloud intelligent structure that allows a low-latency processing and scalable learning. Complex deep learning algorithms are used to learn nonlinear time dependencies between meteorological variables and power generation curves, and uncertainty-aware modeling increases the accuracy of prediction when operating under changing operating conditions. The results of the experiments prove that the offered framework has a high forecasting accuracy and robustness in comparison with traditional machine learning and statistical tools and can be successfully implemented in the next-generation smart grids.

title: AI-Enabled Intrusion Detection in Smart Grids Using Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The growing level of digitalization and connectivity of smart grids has greatly increased the attacker surface, rendering traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) irrelevant in the face of organized and covert assaults. In this paper, the authors provide an AI-based intrusion detection system in smart grids using graph neural networks (GNNs), which explicitly captures the topological and operational relationships between grid elements. The smart grid is modeled as a dynamic graph with the nodes representing substations, intelligent electronic equipment, and meters and edges representing physical and communication interactions. Through the graph-based spatial learning, the proposed model efficiently identifies anomalous behaviors caused by the false information inoculation, denial-of-service and command manipulation attacks. The experimental analysis on benchmark smart-grid cyber-security datasets illustrates that the suggested GNN-based IDS has a high detection accuracy and robustness in contrast toward the traditional ML and DL baselines. The findings indicate the topology-aware learning efficiency in improving cyber resilience of the future intelligent power systems.

title: An Optuna-Optimized XGBoost Framework for Robust Non-Technical Loss Detection in Smart Grids
abstract: This study presents a robust, end-to-end machine learning framework for detecting Non-Technical Losses (NTLs) in smart power grids. The proposed Optimized Bootstrapped Gradient Classifier (OBGC) integrates k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) imputation for missing data handling, Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) for class imbalance correction and Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization. The framework is evaluated using the State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC) dataset comprising 42,373 consumers over 1035 days (January 2014–October 2016), characterized by 25.6% missing values and a severe class imbalance (91.46% honest vs. 8.54% theft-prone consumers). To ensure robust evaluation, all experiments employ stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training set, with a held-out 20% test set reserved for final performance assessment. Experimental results show that OBGC achieves an accuracy of 96.61%, precision of 96.18%, recall of 97.13%, and F1-score of 96.65%, substantially outperforming baseline XGBoost (accuracy 92.75%, F1 36.11%) and other state-of-the-art classifiers. An ablation study confirms that ADASYN is the most critical component; its removal causes recall to collapse from 97.13% to 16.87%, demonstrating the severe impact of class imbalance on theft detection. Optuna-based tuning contributes an additional 3.29 percentage-point gain in accuracy over the unoptimized baseline. The framework offers a transparent, reproducible, and operationally feasible solution for real-world NTL detection.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Power Systems: A Review of Methods, Use Cases, and Future Directions
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
abstract: Modern electrical networks face growing operational demands as electricity consumption rises and renewable generation, distributed resources, and electric vehicles become more common. Artificial intelligence (AI) can learn useful relationships from operating records and simulated data, supporting tasks such as demand prediction, fault identification, state estimation, stability screening, and energy scheduling. This review organizes reported AI techniques and applications in both large interconnected grids and smaller power systems. It considers rule-based and fuzzy approaches alongside machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and newer foundation-model methods. The literature suggests that AI may accelerate selected analyses and provide flexible decision support, but dependable performance still relies on representative data, generalization, explainability, cyber protection, and real-world validation. A staged approach that combines AI with engineering models and expert oversight is outlined. This paper synthesizes existing studies and does not claim new experimental results..

title: A Review and Comparative Analysis of Techniques for Restoring IT System Continuity After Cyberattacks
abstract: Cyberattacks represent one of the key threats to the stability, integrity, and availability of modern information systems, making the rapid and effective restoration of operational continuity after cybersecurity incidents essential. This article provides a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of techniques used to recover systems following information security incidents, including such approaches as backups, redundancy, virtualization, and cloud-based technologies. The analysis draws on an in-depth examination of the academic literature and industry practices, enabling a comparison of the most widely used methods in both historical and contemporary contexts. Particular attention is given to evaluating the effectiveness of these solutions with respect to two critical continuity metrics: system recovery time (RTO) and acceptable data loss (RPO). The comparison also takes into account the economic aspects of implementing and maintaining various technologies, as well as organizational factors influencing the effectiveness of recovery strategies. Both the advantages and limitations of each approach are discussed, with consideration of system scale, resource availability, and the level of process automation. The study identifies significant research gaps in continuity strategies, especially in light of the growing complexity of IT environments and the integration of cloud and hybrid solutions. Based on the analysis, recommendations are formulated for further development of system recovery practices, with particular emphasis on standardizing procedures, automating recovery testing, and adopting emerging security technologies. These findings may serve as a foundation for building more effective and resilient information security strategies, ultimately enhancing data protection and ensuring a higher degree of operational continuity in the face of the increasing volume and complexity of cyberthreats.

title: Designing Resilient Cyber Physical Systems in the Age of AI
abstract: This publication looks at how artificial intelligence will change the design, protection and governance of cyber-physical systems. The contribution discusses trustworthy telemetry, anomaly detection, explainability, false positives, model drift, secure control pathways, command traceability, compliance evidence, and responsible automation. This volume is designed for researchers and product leaders, cybersecurity professionals, engineers and policymakers, students and practitioners working at the intersection of AI, cyber-physical systems, industry security and digital transformation. title: Selecting Aggregate Load Telemetry for Coherent Subregional Demand Reconstruction
venue: IEEE International Conference on Smart Energy Grid Engineering (SEGE)
abstract: Utilities increasingly operate advanced metering and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems. The gap is that high-frequency customer, feeder, and industrial load data are often privacy-sensitive, cyber-sensitive, proprietary, or fragmented across operating companies. Therefore, external planners, statistical offices, investors, and researchers may receive a regional load total and only a small number of aggregate subregional time series. This paper investigates which aggregate load telemetry feeds should be released, audited, or quality-controlled to enable coherent reconstruction of all subregional demands while preserving microdata privacy. We formulate selected aggregate time series as anchors in a softmax-share disaggregation model. We compare five anchor-selection rules: random, largest-demand, highest-variance, feature-diversity, and greedy. All are evaluated against an exhaustive oracle on public power demand datasets. At two anchors, greedy and largest-demand selection match the exhaustive optimum on MISO, ISONE, PJM, and ENTSO-E Italy. Random selection performs worse across all four systems, with weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) differences of 11.7, 13.1, 19.5, and 44.3 percentage points for MISO, ISONE, PJM, and ENTSO-E Italy, respectively. The highest-variance rule is consistently poor. The findings suggest prioritizing releasing or certifying large, structurally informative aggregate load series. Volatility alone is generally weaker.

title: XLTFormer: Regime-Adaptive Time–Frequency Expert Routing for Multi-Step Load and Energy Forecasting
abstract: Multi-step load forecasting remains challenging because real-world demand series exhibit non-stationarity, multi-scale periodicity, and regime-dependent temporal structure. Performance degradation often arises not from insufficient model size alone, but from mismatch between the active operating regime and the inductive bias of a fixed forecasting backbone. This paper proposes XLTFormer, a regime-adaptive framework that treats multi-step prediction as descriptor-augmented routing over heterogeneous structural priors. Memory, attention, decomposition, cross-variable interaction, patch-based representation, and frequency-domain modeling are organized as route-level experts, while the methodological contribution centers on four mechanisms: regime-descriptor-guided sample-level routing, post-mixture peak-context correction, lightweight expert-preserving training, and validation-gated deployment selection. Across three real-load benchmarks, XLTFormer attains the lowest mean error on all five reported metrics under the ten-seed protocol and remains top-ranked overall under the controlled-capacity comparison. In the retained rerun, the final deployment repeatedly selects the cross-variable route on all three datasets, with WAPE/sMAPE values of 3.7274/3.7320 on Electricity, 3.9576/3.8643 on PJM, and 7.2619/7.5058 on GEFCom2014 Load. Relative to the strongest competing baseline, the WAPE improvement reaches 2.11% on Electricity, 1.11% on PJM, and 1.02% on GEFCom2014 Load, while the corresponding sMAPE reduction reaches 2.40%, 1.29%, and 1.08%, respectively. Seed-level paired tests, dependence-aware block bootstrap, and Friedman ranking analysis further show that this retained deployment advantage is stable rather than incidental. The temporal-routing audit nevertheless indicates that the sample-level gate still redistributes route responsibility across local regimes, especially when peak, ramp, or weather-linked stress increases. These results show that the practical forecasting gain comes from the full reliability-oriented framework, in which adaptive routing shapes route interaction and validation-gated selection determines the final retained output, rather than from attributing the deployed accuracy to raw adaptive fusion alone. Overall, the framework provides an effective direction for accurate, stable, and practically relevant multi-step load forecasting.

title: Differentially Private Time Series Publishing Based on Multiscale Wavelet Energy Features and Noise Covariance Matrix Optimization
abstract: To address the distortion of temporal trends and structures caused by differential privacy noise, this paper proposes a differentially private time-series release method based on multiscale energy features and noise covariance optimization, termed Wavelet Energy and Covariance Optimization-Based Differential Privacy (WECO-DP). The proposed method normalizes time series using fixed public bounds and employs public calibration data separate from the protected input to predetermine scale-specific energy weights, fixed coefficient positions, and the number of retained coefficients at each scale, thereby constructing a fixed wavelet query. Under an adjacency relation defined by a change at a single time point, worst-case sensitivity constraints are established by analyzing the responses of the fixed query to changes at different time positions. The scale-specific energy weights are then incorporated into the noise optimization objective to jointly determine the Gaussian noise variances across scales. Subsequently, a single Gaussian perturbation is applied to the retained wavelet coefficients, and the released series is obtained through the inverse discrete wavelet transform. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that WECO-DP satisfies event-level (ε,δ)-differential privacy. Experimental results on three real-world time-series datasets involving water consumption, electricity consumption, and unemployment rates show that WECO-DP generally achieves lower root mean square error and mean absolute error than five baseline methods under different privacy budgets. Ablation experiments and structure-preservation analysis further demonstrate the contributions of fixed coefficient selection, scale-specific energy weighting, and scale-specific noise variance optimization to release utility. WECO-DP reduces the influence of privacy perturbation on the principal structural information of time series while satisfying event-level privacy constraints, thereby improving the utility of the released data.

title: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment and Detection in Smart Grid Infrastructure
venue: International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering
abstract: Smart grids represent the next generation of power systems where electricity networks are integrated with digital communication technologies, distributed energy resources, and intelligent monitoring devices. The adoption of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI), Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, phasor measurement units (PMUs), and Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensors enables utilities to monitor and control power systems in real time. While these technologies significantly improve operational efficiency and grid reliability, they also introduce new cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can threaten the stability of critical energy infrastructure. Cyber-attacks such as false data injection attacks, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, coordinated control attacks, and stealthy command manipulation in SCADA environments can disrupt grid operations, cause large-scale outages, and compromise sensitive operational data.This paper proposes an artificial intelligence–driven cybersecurity risk detection framework designed for modern smart grid infrastructures. The proposed framework integrates data from multiple grid components including SCADA systems, smart meters, PMUs, and network communication logs. A hybrid detection approach combining machine learning–based anomaly detection with graph-based threat propagation analysis is developed to identify abnormal operational patterns and potential cyber intrusion events. The framework further incorporates probabilistic risk propagation modeling to estimate the potential cascading impact of detected threats across interconnected grid components.Experimental validation using benchmark power system datasets demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly improves detection accuracy and reduces false alarm rates compared to traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems. The proposed framework supports real-time monitoring and provides utilities with a proactive mechanism for identifying cybersecurity threats before they escalate into major operational disruptions. This research contributes toward strengthening the resilience and security of future cyber-physical energy systems.

title: Multi-Step Load Forecasting with State-Guided Expert Routing for Energy Management Systems
abstract: Accurate load forecasting is crucial for operational planning and rolling decision-making in energy management systems (EMSs). However, the dynamic nature of temporal patterns and the inconsistent availability of covariates across the forecasting horizon complicate this task. While covariate-aware Transformer models distinguish between endogenous and exogenous inputs, their feed-forward modules typically employ homogeneous transformations across different operating conditions, and traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing mechanisms usually rely solely on implicit token representations for decision-making. To address these limitations, we propose SA-TimeXer-MoHE, a scenario-aware TimeXer model with heterogeneous experts. First, the model partitions its inputs by forecast-time availability into the load target, historical-only measurements, deterministic future calendar variables, and operating-scenario covariates. Then, it replaces the homogeneous feed-forward module with MLP, depthwise-convolution, drift, and residual experts and conditions sparse Top-K routing jointly on token representations and nine EMS scenario variables. On a real EMS dataset, the full model achieves reported mean MAE, RMSE, P95_AE, and Ramp_MAE values that are 7.4%, 5.7%, 4.0%, and 6.0% lower, respectively, than those of TimeXer across 1, 2, 4, and 8 h forecasting horizons. These results highlight the potential of SA-TimeXer-MoHE as a forecasting component for rolling scheduling, peak regulation, and storage dispatch in practical EMS applications.

title: Smart Renewable Energy Microgrid Framework for Rural Electrification Integrating Digital Twin Modeling, IoT Monitoring, Predictive Analytics, and Edge-Cloud Computing
venue: Advances in Electrical and Computer Engineering
abstract: Access to stable electricity supply for rural areas is still a daunting task due to the factors such as the instability of the grid, inadequate infrastructure, poor power quality and lack of intelligent energy management systems. While renewable energy-based microgrids are seen as potential solutions to the problem, most of the existing ones run as independent power systems with very little monitoring, reactive maintenance approach and little optimization capability. The proposed system involves the design and development of an intelligent edge-cloud renewable energy microgrid architecture that incorporates advanced power conversion, monitoring, prediction, and optimization systems within a single framework for sustainable self-sufficiency in rural areas. The architecture encompasses photovoltaic power generation, battery energy storage, dynamic reconfigurable photovoltaic array, seven-level reduced switch multi-level inverter, Internet of Things (IoT) based monitoring system, cloud computing-based data acquisition and digital twin models. Electrical and environmental parameters are continuously acquired through distributed sensor nodes and transmitted via Raspberry Pi using Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) and cloud communication protocols. The proposed architecture offers improved power quality, enhanced monitoring capability, predictive maintenance support, intelligent energy allocation, and scalability for future rural electrification and Microgrid-as-a-Service applications.

title: Metering Device Status Topology Perception and Fault Propagation Risk Warning Integrating a Graph Attention Network
venue: IEEE International Conference on Power, Electronics and Computer Applications (ICPECA)
abstract: With the large-scale deployment of metering devices in smart grids, traditional single-device status monitoring methods struggle to effectively capture the complex topological relationships between devices and the resulting cross-device fault propagation risks. To address this issue, this paper proposes a solution that incorporates a Graph Attention Network (GAT). This paper first abstracts the metering device network into a graph structure and then introduces the GAT model, which boasts topology awareness and explicit modeling of propagation paths. Finally, a fault propagation risk warning model is constructed. Experimental results show that in the propagation path tracing experiment, the critical path recall rate reached 92.8%, and the source localization accuracy (SLA) reached 100%. In the cascading fault warning timeliness experiment, the average warning lead time was 55.2 minutes, with an overall standard deviation of only 8.3 minutes. The results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively enhance the resilience and security protection capabilities of smart grid metering systems, providing a feasible path for the early prevention and control of correlated faults.

title: Coordinated Optimization Strategy for Distribution Network Voltage Control Based on an Information-Energy Integrated Centralized Control System
venue: IEEE International Conference on Power, Electronics and Computer Applications (ICPECA)
abstract: The stochastic and intermittent nature of high-penetration distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation poses severe challenges to distribution network voltage stability. To address the limitations of traditional Automatic Voltage Control (AVC) systems, such as slow response, lack of coordination, and insufficient situational awareness, this paper proposes a novel coordinated optimization framework based on a new-generation Information-Energy Integrated Centralized Control System (MCS). Leveraging the MCS's capabilities for panoramic monitoring of primary and auxiliary equipment and multi-station data fusion, a “Cloud-Edge-Terminal” three-layer control architecture is established. Data penetration services of the MCS aggregate system-wide electrical measurements, equipment status, and environmental data. A Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model is formulated with the objective of minimizing voltage deviation and network losses, which is efficiently solved using a Modified Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization (MDPSO) algorithm incorporating a simulated annealing mechanism. Finally, utilizing the inherent inter-station joint anti-maloperation and sequential control operation invocation functions of the MCS, remote, secure, and automated closed-loop control of On-Load Tap Changer (OLTC) positions and reactive power compensation device switching is realized. Simulation results based on a practical regional distribution network demonstrate that, compared to traditional AVC, the proposed strategy increases the voltage qualification rate from 95.8% to 99.2%, reduces average network losses by 12.7%, shortens the control response time to within 10 seconds, and maintains high control reliability even under communication congestion scenarios. This significantly enhances the voltage quality, operational economy, and resilience of distribution networks with high penetration of renewable energy.

title: From accurate AI to sustainable AI: A lifecycle computational framework for resource-efficient, explainable, and trustworthy artificial intelligence in energy systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to improve forecasting, optimization, control, and decision support in energy systems, yet much of the literature remains dominated by accuracy-centric evaluation. This critical review argues that such evaluation is insufficient for sustainable energy transitions because AI models also impose computational, environmental, operational, and governance costs across their lifecycle. Rather than descriptively summarizing prior work, the paper comparatively examines major groups of studies, including AI for renewable-energy forecasting, smart-grid optimization, energy management, Green AI, explainable AI, and trustworthy AI, to identify where their assumptions, metrics, and deployment priorities converge or conflict. The review shows that existing research often treats model performance, computational efficiency, carbon footprint, explainability, robustness, privacy, and accountability as separate concerns, leaving a gap in integrated lifecycle assessment. To address this gap, the paper proposes a lifecycle computational framework for sustainable AI in energy systems, covering data acquisition, model design, training, inference, deployment, monitoring, retraining, and governance. The framework supports multi-dimensional evaluation of AI systems in terms of accuracy, resource efficiency, carbon impact, transparency, reliability, and real-world deployability, offering a pathway from merely accurate AI toward sustainable, explainable, and trustworthy AI for energy applications.

title: AUAKE-SG: An ASCON-based ultra-lightweight authenticated key exchange scheme for smart grids
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
abstract: Communication between smart meters (SMs) and neighborhood area network (NAN) gateways in smart grids often takes place over public channels, exposing these links to impersonation, traceability, replay, and physical-capture-assisted attacks. Authentication protocols for this setting must provide clearly defined security guarantees within the limited computational resources of smart meters. This paper introduces AUAKE-SG, an Authenticated Sponge Construction (ASCON)-based ultra-lightweight authenticated key exchange scheme that supports mutual authentication, session-key establishment, and privacy preservation with low overhead. Its security is evaluated through informal attack analysis, automated ProVerif verification, and proofs in the Random Oracle Model (ROM). A crash-consistent per-meter encryption counter prevents operational reuse of request-nonce inputs under the long-term key, subject to the protected-state assumption, and eliminates the need for runtime random-number generation at the meter. AUAKE-SG completes authentication in two messages with a communication cost of 1408 bits (176 bytes). Its estimated cryptographic processing cost is 0.050389 ms for the adopted Raspberry Pi 4/desktop profile, comprising 0.032089 ms at the SM and 0.018300 ms at the NAN. These results indicate a balanced security–efficiency profile for the evaluated SM–NAN setting.

title: AFERNet: Adaptive Frequency-Band Expert Routing for Nonstationary Electricity Load Forecasting
abstract: Electricity load series combine strong daily and weekly harmonics with drifting levels and growing sub-daily variability, and the deep models that handle this best are often costly to retrain. We present AFERNet, a lightweight forecaster that normalizes each look-back window, splits its real Fourier spectrum into <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K$ </tex-math></inline-formula> contiguous bands, reconstructs each band in the time domain, predicts it with a channel-independent linear expert, and fuses the experts with softmax weights computed from log band energies. At <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K=3$ </tex-math></inline-formula> the model has <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$1.5\times $ </tex-math></inline-formula> the parameters of DLinear plus a 59-parameter gate. We evaluate it against DLinear, PatchTST, iTransformer, FreTS, and five classical baselines on ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Electricity, and a fully specified GEFCom2014 zonal-load series under one protocol: validation-based learning-rate selection with the same grid for every model, three seeds per configuration, and errors in both standardized and original units including peak-period error. The central finding is negative for the adaptive mechanism: routing-isolation controls show that a learned input-independent gate, and even a uniform gate, match the adaptive gate within seed noise on all tracks tested, the gate weights vary by less than ±0.02 across test windows, and the gain over DLinear is explained by instance normalization. AFERNet has the lowest or tied-lowest horizon-averaged error on ETTh1 (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$0.4446\pm 0.0014$ </tex-math></inline-formula> MSE), ETTh2 (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$0.3759\pm 0.0019$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, separated from iTransformer at 0.3831), and ETTm2, trails PatchTST in MSE on ETTm1, is the least accurate of the five on the 321-client Electricity panel (where iTransformer leads by 23% MSE), and is tied with DLinear on GEFCom2014 (16.23 versus 16.22 MW MAE), where every deep model beats the operational classical baselines but a linear regression with realized temperature is better at the weekly horizon. A physically defined band split at the daily period, which reduces to a daily/sub-daily two-expert model, is the most accurate band rule on ETTh1 and ETTh2. AFERNet keeps the parameter count, training time, and memory of a linear model at 321 channels, where PatchTST is 20–<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$60\times $ </tex-math></inline-formula> more expensive in time, but its single-window latency on seven-channel data is about <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$4\times $ </tex-math></inline-formula> that of DLinear.
